purpose:
LGA Corporate Peer Challenge Action Plan
following full report and recommendations.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
Local
authorities were expected to undertake a peer challenge at least
once every five years, supporting the Council in meeting its Best
Value Duty under the Local Government Act 1999 to “make
arrangements to secure continuous improvement in the way in which
its functions are exercised, having regard to a combination of
economy, efficiency and effectiveness”. It also provided
ongoing external assurance following the conclusion of government
intervention two years ago and contributes to the Councils
continued progress towards becoming an outstanding
council.
 
At the
conclusion of Sandwell Council’s CPC, the LGA set out
expected timelines for the publication of their final report
(within three months) and for an action plan to respond to the
recommendations (within five months). The report was published in
March 2026, within the expected timeframe. The action plan was
therefore expected to be developed and published by no later than
22 June 2026. Since the receipt of the Peer Team's final report,
the Council had been developing the actions to respond to the
recommendations - in many cases this was a development or
realignment of existing activities to address known areas for
improvement. Following the local elections in May 2026 and the
change of dates for Cabinet meetings, in agreement from the LGA
publication of the Action Plan had been deferred to July 2026 to
allow for consideration by Cabinet at its July meeting.
 
The
peer team’s initial feedback described Sandwell’s
progress over recent years as “remarkable.” Their
reflections were overwhelmingly positive, noting how genuinely
moved they were by the passion and energy demonstrated by everyone
they met.
 
The
report identified that the peer team found that Sandwell Council
had undergone a remarkable organisational, cultural and leadership
transformation. The peer team found a council that was now
credible, confident, professional and ambitious, widely recognised
by partners and staff as fundamentally different from the
organisation that was previously under Government intervention.
Staff described a dramatic positive shift in culture, behaviours
and morale.
 
The
peer team recognised the substantial improvement achieved but
emphasised the need to maintain momentum. Stating a continued focus
on culture, governance safeguards, and high-quality recruitment
will be essential to avoid regression. The Council’s ambition
to be “outstanding” was highlighted as commendable, but
it was noted that further work was needed to define what
“outstanding” means for Sandwell’s services,
outcomes, and communities. Overall, the peer team reported strong
evidence that the Council was well positioned to meet the
borough’s challenges, with a motivated workforce and
leadership committed to sustained improvement.
 

Alternative Options Considered
An
alternative option would be to not to complete and approve an
action plan to respond to the recommendations from the Peer Review.
Without a comprehensive and overarching action plan to track
activity and accountability, there would be no assurance mechanism
to ensure progress or opportunity to align existing activity
towards improvement. This would not support the Council’s
journey to ’outstanding’. It would also be a risk to
the Council being able to demonstrate it was delivering its Best
Value Duty. This option was not recommended.
 
Resolved:-  
 

(1) 
that approval is given to the Local Government
Association Corporate Peer Challenge 2026 Action Plan and
associated governance and monitoring arrangements to oversee
delivery and ensure achievement of the Council’s improvement
objectives;
 

(2) 
that Cabinet recognise that the Local Government
Association will conduct a follow up visit in late Autumn
2026.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Local Government Association Corporate Peer Challenge 2026 Action Plan to ensure continuous improvement and meet the Council's improvement objectives.

purpose:
Approval is sought for a Direct Award. The
contracts related to cremator equipment, servicing and repairs are
due to end on 31 August 2026. Also following the release of the new
process guidance note for Crematoria PG5/2(25) from DEFRA in
December 2025 which identifies the most effective technologies and
processes for limiting and monitoring emissions to air from
crematoria, Sandwell as a cremation authority needs to invest in
new equipment at both its crematoria by December 2029 in order to
be compliant with the new statutory guidance. The council’s
current provider Facultatieve Technologies (FT) is a market leader
in this field both in terms of the suppling equipment such as
cremators and associated ancillary equipment (such as mercury
abatement equipment) and undertaking ongoing service, maintenance
and repairs.

Previous tender exercises have seen very few bids received with FT
in some instances being the only bidder. In order to have the
necessary contracts in place for the supply of the new equipment
necessary to be compliant with the new statutory regulations and
ongoing servicing and maintenance requirements for cremator
equipment in Sandwell, it is proposed a direct contract award is
made to Facultatieve Technologies.

Combined expenditure for the duration of a four-year contract to
include new equipment is expected to be circa
£1,500,000.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
Council operated two crematoria sites in West Bromwich and Rowley
Regis, delivering approximately 3,000 cremations each year. These
were essential local services supporting residents at a sensitive
time, and continuity, reliability and compliance were critical to
maintaining public confidence.
 
The
existing contract for the provision of cremator equipment,
servicing, maintenance and repairs expired on 31 August 2026. The
market for these services was highly specialised, with a very
limited number of providers nationally. Facultatieve Technologies was the current provider,
a recognised market leader, and the supplier of the Council’s
existing crematoria infrastructure. The technical requirement for
compatibility with installed equipment, alongside warranty and
servicing constraints, significantly limited the viability of
alternative providers.
 
In
December 2025, DEFRA issued updated statutory guidance (PG5/2(25)),
requiring crematoria operators to install mercury and nitrogen
oxide abatement technology by December 2029. While Sandwell Valley
Crematorium had partial compliance, neither site fully met the new
requirements. The proposed contract incorporated the installation
of the necessary abatement systems, ensuring regulatory compliance
within the required timeframe.
 
Bringing equipment supply, installation, servicing, maintenance
and regulatory upgrades within a single contractual arrangement
provided a coherent and controlled approach to service delivery,
strengthened accountability, and reduced operational risk. Cost
estimates were informed by historic spend and supplier quotations
and were considered proportionate to the scale and technical
complexity of the requirement.
 
Given
the limited supplier market, previous procurement outcomes, and the
need to ensure operational continuity and compliance, the direct
award via an established framework represents the most robust and
deliverable option.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1: Undertake a full open procurement process. This option would
involve testing the wider market through a competitive tender
exercise. While this could, in principle, demonstrate openness and
competition, previous procurements in 2018 and 2022 resulted in
only a single compliant bid, requiring exemptions to proceed. There
remained a significant risk that alternative suppliers would be
unable to support existing equipment or meet compatibility
requirements, creating service, warranty and compliance risks.
Given the low likelihood of a different outcome and the potential
for disruption, this option was not recommended.
 
Option
2: In house provision . This option
would effectively require the Council to have the technical
expertise and experience to install the new abatement equipment and
be able to service and maintain this and all associated cremator
equipment. The Council did not have the knowledge and expertise
internally to undertake this work and given the limited
amount of companies who undertake this
would be unlikely to be able to recruit individual to do so in a
cost effective manner. The existing
equipment and the new abatement equipment was provided by FT which
was all compatible and subject to FTs warranties and guarantees.
Not using FT to maintain and repair this equipment would also
invalidate these warranties. This option was not recommended given
the technical expertise and experience necessary, along with an
ongoing need for equipment supplies, to undertake complex
maintenance of the cremators which suggests the contracting of this
work to the manufacturer was the most appropriate approach to
ensure crematoria services in Sandwell can reliably be
maintained.
 
Option
3: Cease provision of crematoria services. This option would
involve the Council exiting the direct provision of crematoria
services entirely. Whilst the service was not a statutory duty, it
was an established and heavily utilised local service, delivering
approximately 3,000 cremations annually and generating income for
the Council. Withdrawal would have significant reputational,
community and operational implications, including reduced access to
local bereavement services. This option was not
recommended.
 
Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that approval is given for the award of a four-year
contract, commencing 1 September 2026, for the provision of
cremator equipment, associated ancillary supplies, installation,
maintenance, servicing and repairs, to Facultatieve Technologies via the Yorkshire
Purchasing Organisation (YPO) Framework 1032, on the basis that
this represents a compliant and appropriate procurement route under
the Procurement Act 2023 and the Council’s Contract Procedure
Rules;
 

(2) 
that the total contract value of up to £1.5m,
comprising both revenue and capital elements, is approved within
the Council’s existing budget framework, with the capital
element subject to formal inclusion within the approved capital
programme;
 

(3) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director – Finance and Transformation, in consultation with
the Service Director of Governance and Monitoring Officer, to take
all actions necessary to give effect to recommendations (1) and (2)
above.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to award a four-year contract for cremator equipment provision, maintenance, and repairs to Facultatieve Technologies.

purpose:
To consider the Crisis and Resilience Fund
2026/27-2028/29
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
In the
June 2025 Spending Review, the Government announced a new Crisis
and Resilience Fund (CRF), launching in April 2026.
 
The
CRF was a national government grant-funded programme, introduced by
the Department for Work and Pensions, partly to replace the
previous Department for Work and Pensions’ Household Support
Fund (HSF) and Discretionary Housing Payments (DHP) schemes, both
of which were administered by local authorities.
 
HSF
was used to support financially vulnerable households with
essential costs relating to energy, food and water, and wider
essential costs. The scheme ended on 31 March 2026.
 
DHP
was used to help residents to cover the cost of a deposit on a new
property or help with a shortfall in rent or removal costs. This
support also ended on 31 March 2026.
 
Entering into the Crisis and Resilience Fund grant arrangements would provide
the Council with significant funding to support vulnerable
residents and strengthen local welfare and resilience services.
This funding enabled the Council to deliver targeted support,
address financial hardship and develop longer?term preventative
approaches in line with national requirements, while ensuring
compliance with grant conditions and enabling timely implementation
of services.
 
The
DWP published statutory guidance in January 2026 outlining the
purpose of the CRF, eligible expenditure and delivery expectations
for local authorities.
 
The
CRF provided a three-year, ring-fenced funding settlement to enable
local authorities to support residents experiencing financial
hardship while also investing in longer term financial resilience
and prevention.
 
The
CRF ran from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2029. The CRF was intended to
provide immediate support to households experiencing financial
shocks whilst reducing future demand for crisis intervention
through investment in financial resilience, advice and
community?based support.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Continue expenditure as per the previous Household
Support Fund, allocating a proportion of funding to free school
meal holiday vouchers – Not recommended. This option would
continue the provision of free school meal vouchers to all eligible
families during school holidays, which was previously aligned to
the (now-discontinued) government grant-funded Household Support
Fund programme. Whilst this would provide short-term support, it
would not align with the primary objectives of the new CRF grant
conditions, which required a significant focus on crisis
intervention and building long-term financial resilience. The CRF
was an entirely separate scheme which required local authorities to
address both ‘crisis’ and
‘resilience’. Universal voucher provision in many cases
did not meet the definition of ‘crisis provision’, it
did not address the underlying causes of financial hardship and it would reduce funding available for
preventative and resilience-building support. This option was
therefore not recommended. The Council would continue to provide
targeted crisis support, including emergency food assistance and
crisis payments, to ensure families experiencing hardship can
access support when needed.
 
Option
2 – Deliver the programme primarily through the voluntary and
community sector – Not recommended. This option would
allocate a significant proportion of funding to voluntary and
community sector organisations for delivery. Whilst this could
extend community reach, it would reduce the Council’s ability
to maintain strategic oversight, monitor performance, and redirect
resources in response to emerging needs. It also presented risks
relating to provider capacity, consistency of delivery and
equitable access across the borough. This option was therefore not
recommended.

Corporate Services, to determine a set of ‘resilience

purpose:
The report sets out the outturn position for
the 2025/26 financial year for both revenue and capital
budgets.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
Section 151 of the 1972 Local Government Act required the Chief
Financial Officer to ensure the proper administration of the
Council’s financial affairs. Budgetary control, which
includes the regular monitoring and reporting of budgets is an
essential element in discharging this statutory responsibility. The
reporting and analysis of financial performance versus budget
supports the financial sustainability of the Council.
 

Alternative Options Considered
There
were no alternative options to consider.
 
Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that the outturn position for the 2025/26 financial
year is received and referred to the Budget and Corporate Scrutiny
Management Board for consideration and comment;
 

(2) 
that the Revenue Budget underspend of
(£2.741m) for the General Fund is acknowledged and
noted
 

(3) 
that the following variances from budget in relation
to ring-fenced funding are acknowledged and noted:

·      
an overspend of £11.589m for the Dedicated
Schools Grant

·      
an overspend of £1.098m for the Housing
Revenue Account
 

(4) 
that approval is given for the transfers to and from
General Fund and Schools reserves, totalling £14.053m (net
transfer to reserves), for the 2025/26 financial year, as set out
in Appendix C;
 
 

(5) 
that approval is given for a transfer of
£1.098m from the Housing Revenue Account reserve in order to offset the corresponding overspend, on
completion of the financial closedown process.
 

(6) 
that is respect of the Capital Programme, approval
is given for the addition of £1.208m UK Shared Prosperity
Fund grant received from the West Midlands Combined Authority into
the General Fund Capital Programme for 2025/26, to fund associated
project expenditure incurred;
 

(7) 
that is respect of the Capital Programme, approval
is given for the addition of £4.606m Devolved Formula Capital
grant funding received from the Department for Education into the
General Fund Capital Programme for 2025/26, to fund corresponding
schools capital expenditure
incurred.
 

(8)

(9)

Account of £62.330m, as per Appendix E, representing 67% of
the revised budget for 2025/26 is received.

purpose:

content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
Council’s Corporate Performance Report enabled the Council to
track progress in delivering the strategic outcomes in the Council
Plan, improve services through identifying poor performance and
sharing good practice, celebrate the Councils achievements and
where things were going well and provide a strong evidence base for

Through identifying opportunities for continuous improvement, the

Councils journey to becoming an outstanding
organisation.
 

Alternative Options Considered
There

Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that the progress in delivering the Council Plan
2024-2027 is noted and approval is given to the 2025/26 Quarter 4
and Annual monitoring report.
 

(2) 
that approval is given to the changes to the
Corporate Performance Indicators outlined in Appendix A.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve progress in delivering the Council Plan 2024-2027 and changes to Corporate Performance Indicators.

purpose:
This policy sets out our framework for
responding to anti-social behaviour (ASB). It defines ASB,
describes our approach to addressing incidents, explains the
reporting process, outlines the guiding principles that inform our
actions, and details the enforcement procedures.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
Anti?social behaviour could disproportionately affect people who
were already vulnerable and could escalate quickly if not addressed
effectively. A clear, shared policy framework was essential to
ensure responses were timely, proportionate and focused on reducing
harm.
 
The
Council had statutory duties and powers under the Anti?Social
Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, including responsibilities
relating to enforcement, safeguarding, partnership working and the
Case Review (Community Trigger) process.
 
The
adoption of a formal ASB Policy was necessary to ensure that the
Council’s response to anti?social behaviour was structured,
consistent and capable of demonstrating a clear focus on the impact
of behaviour on victims and communities. It provided a defined
framework within which cases were assessed, ensuring that decisions
were informed by evidence, applied proportionately and supported by
appropriate consideration of vulnerability, safeguarding and
equality duties. In doing so, the policy strengthened transparency
for residents, supported consistent expectations across services,
and enabled the Council to evidence that its approach was fair,
reasoned and in accordance with statutory and regulatory
requirements.
 
The
policy supported a balanced approach, combining early intervention,
prevention and support with enforcement action where behaviour was
persistent, serious or places others at risk.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Continue to manage anti?social behaviour through existing
statutory powers, service procedures and partnership arrangements
without adopting a single, consolidated policy framework. Under
this approach, the Council would retain discretion in its response
to ASB but without a formally adopted and published framework
setting out how that discretion was to be exercised across
services. In the absence of a formal policy, there would be an
increased likelihood of inconsistency in decision?making, reduced
transparency for residents and partners, and greater exposure to
complaint, challenge or findings of maladministration. It would
also weaken the Council’s ability to demonstrate compliance
with statutory guidance and Housing Ombudsman
expectations.
 
Resolved that approval is given to the
Anti?Social Behaviour (ASB) Policy for implementation across
Housing and Community Safety services.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Anti-Social Behaviour (ASB) Policy for implementation across Housing and Community Safety services.

purpose:
Cabinet approval is required for several
Housing Policies.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
A
Self-Assessment against the Regulator of Social Housing Consumer
Standards (September 2024, refreshed February 2026) identified the
need to strengthen governance and strategic oversight through a
clearer and more comprehensive suite of housing management
policies.
 
In
response, the Council had developed a programme of policy reviews
to ensure services are supported by up-to-date, consistent, and
compliant policies across key areas of housing
management.
 
Several policies were also driven by specific legislative
requirements, including new duties arising from the Renters’
Rights Act 2025 and existing requirements under housing
legislation.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1: Do Nothing Not progressing the policy updates would leave gaps
or outdated policies in place, increasing the risk of
non-compliance, inconsistent service delivery, and regulatory
challenge. This option was rejected.
 
Option
2: Partial Policy Update Updating only selected policies was
considered but would not provide a consistent or comprehensive
framework. This option was also rejected.
 
Resolved approval is given to the
following polices:
 

a.   
E-Scooter and E Bike Policy;

b.   
Mutual Exchange Policy;

c.    
Learning and Development Policy;

d.   
Garage Lettings Policy;

e.   
Property Succession Policy;

f.     
Abandoned Goods Policy.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations to strengthen housing management policies.

purpose:
Approval needed on some of the specific
processes following the Renters Rights Act being introduced on May
1st and some accompanying policies.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
private rented sector played a significant role in meeting housing
need in Sandwell, but it also presents ongoing challenges relating
to property condition, management standards, tenant rights and
compliance with housing legislation.
 
Recent
housing reform, including the Renters’ Rights Act, had
significantly expanded the Council’s enforcement
responsibilities. These included new offences, higher statutory
maximum penalties of up to £40,000 for some breaches, and
circumstances where enforcement action was mandatory rather than
discretionary.
 
In
this context, it was essential that the Council could demonstrate
that enforcement decisions were made in accordance with statutory
guidance, were applied consistently through a clear and transparent
methodology, were proportionate to the seriousness of the offence,
and could withstand legal scrutiny. Appropriate safeguards,
governance arrangements and equality considerations must also be
embedded within the decision-making process.
 
The
Enforcement Policy therefore provided a structured framework to
explain when civil financial penalties would be used as an
alternative to prosecution, how penalty levels would be calculated,
and the factors that would be taken into
account, including aggravating and mitigating circumstances
and statutory caps. It also ensured that enforcement activity was
undertaken in accordance with the Regulators’ Code, supports
effective deterrence of non-compliance, particularly in cases of
repeat or deliberate offending, and reduces legal and reputational
risk to the Council.
 
Adoption of the policy ensured the Council was appropriately
equipped to discharge its statutory enforcement duties and
implement new housing legislation in a lawful, transparent and
robust manner.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Not to
adopt a formal Enforcement Policy. This was not recommended, as it
would reduce transparency and consistency in decision-making,
increase exposure to legal challenge, and weaken the
Council’s ability to demonstrate compliance with statutory
guidance and its enforcement responsibilities, including those
arising from recent legislative reforms.
 
Resolved that approval is given for
the adoption of the Private Rented Sector and Housing Standards
Enforcement Policy, to provide the formal framework for the
Council’s exercise of its statutory housing enforcement
powers.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt the Private Rented Sector and Housing Standards Enforcement Policy to address challenges in the private rented sector in Sandwell.

purpose:
The report seeks cabinet approval to award
essential contracts in relation to the repair and maintenance of
the council housing stock.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
A
strategic review of Housing Revenue Account Asset Management
contracts had identified several contracts approaching expiry
during 2026/27. The Council was required to ensure that suitable
contractual arrangements remained in place to maintain service
continuity, deliver statutory compliance obligations and provide
value for money in the management of approximately 28,000 homes and
associated housing assets.
 
The
review had also identified the need to procure additional contracts
to provide specialist support to deliver the requirements of the
Building Safety Act and support the Council in meeting its
statutory landlord obligations, regulatory requirements and the
expectations of the Regulator of Social Housing.
 
The
range of contracts seeking delegated authority to procure would
replace existing contracts and, where appropriate, aggregate
requirements into larger strategic arrangements designed to improve
value for money, strengthen supply chain resilience and reduce
contract management complexity. The strategic approach to reducing
the number of contracts into higher value, longer term contracts
would ensure local supply chain of materials and skills were tied
into Sandwell contracts and this in turn would increase the
viability of contractor support due to the stable financial
commitment.
 
Given
the scale, value and programme of procurement activity required,
delegated authority would enable procurement exercises to be
completed in a timely manner, avoiding contract expiry risk whilst
ensuring compliance with the Procurement Act 2023 and the Council's
constitutional governance arrangements.
 
The
proposed contractual arrangements would support delivery of the
Council's housing priorities by ensuring homes remain safe,
compliant, well maintained and fit for purpose, maintaining
regulatory compliance, supporting delivery of building safety
obligations and protecting both residents and housing
assets.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Not re-procure expiring contracts for the identified
works. This would mean that ‘ad hoc’ arrangements would
be required to maintain the Councils housing stock to the required
Decent Homes Standards, Consumer Standards prescribed and directed
by the Regulator for Social Housing including meeting the Consumer
Standards, and all regulatory requirements under the Social Housing
(Regulation) Act 2023, The Housing and Regeneration Act 2008 and
the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018. This could lead
to dissatisfaction amongst tenants, disrepair to housing stock, and
potential sanctions or further regulatory downgrading from the
Regulator of Social Housing. This option was not
progressed.
 
Option
2 – only use in-house provision. Current in-house provision
did not have the capacity to maintain the pace of demand or the
specialist technical provision to carry out all the specialist
works. Therefore, support from external contractors was required to
effectively and compliantly manage all the requirements of the
service. Failure to procure the relevant contracts would impact on
delivering against the Asset Management and Compliance Strategy
potentially leaving housing unsafe, or residents and workers at
risk. This option was not progressed.
 
Option
3 – Spot purchasing outside of a contract agreement.
Purchasing outside of contractual agreement would increase costs
and add cost uncertainty. Also purchasing the types of works
required at the estimated values would not be compliant to the
Councils current Contracts and Procurement Procedure Rules and
could result in works being purchased that did not comply to
stringent controls that were applied during a compliant procurement
of works. This option was not progressed.
 
Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director of Place, in consultation with the Executive Director of
Finance and Transformation, to prepare tender documentation,
conduct a compliant procurement process and award contracts
for:
 

a.   
Delivery of repairs and Maintenance Services;
and

b.   
supply of Building Materials; and

c.    
Delivery of Voids Repairs and Post Tenancy Repairs
Services; and

d.   
Delivery and assurance of Building Safety and
Compliance Services, including High Risk Residential Blocks;
and

e.   
Servicing and Repairs to Lifts.
 
to
the most advantageous tender(s) in accordance with the Procurement
Act 2023, the Procurement Regulations 2024 and the Council’s
Contracts and Procurement Procedure Rules within the approved
budget envelope and in accordance with the Council’s capital
and revenue governance arrangements in relation to the repairs and
maintenance operations within Asset Management.
 

(2) 
that delegated authority is given to the Monitoring
Officer, Service Director - Governance to complete, execute, seal
and take all actions necessary to give effect to the decisions
contained within the report submitted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to delegate authority for the procurement of contracts for housing maintenance and building safety services in Sandwell.

purpose:
The Council requires a reliable, consistent
and technically compliant supply of coated road stone, aggregates,
asphalt materials, ready-mixed concrete and instant road repair
materials to support highway maintenance, planned works, reactive
repairs and emergency reinstatements.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
Council had a statutory duty to maintain the adopted highway.
Well-maintained highways were critical to road safety. Inadequate
maintenance could lead to increased road traffic accidents, reduced
pedestrian safety, congestion, public dissatisfaction, and
reputational damage to the authority.
 
The
council’s in-house Highways Maintenance Team, based at
Taylors Lane Depot, provided a mainly reactive service focused on
fault response and urgent repairs. Although Sandwell had access to
machinery which could produce asphalt in house, additional
materials were required.
 
An
open procurement exercise would be undertaken, and the intention
was to appoint suppliers, based on an agreed pricing schedule, to
ensure value for money. The procurement would be structured into
separate lots, and the Council reserved the right to award one or
more lots to a single supplier or to multiple suppliers. This
approach was intended to support competition, supply resilience and
value for money, and was consistent with procurement best
practice.
 
The
collaborative procurement with Dudley Council was be governed by an
appropriate inter-authority agreement setting out roles and
responsibilities, including (where applicable) which authority
would act as the lead contracting authority, how liabilities would
be apportioned, and how contract management would be
undertaken.
 
The
contract evaluation would be weighted 80% on price and 20% on
quality. The quality criteria would have emphasis on compliance
with health and safety standards and the delivery of social value
in accordance with the council’s priorities.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Do
Nothing. If the Council did not proceed with the proposed Contract,
it would fail to meet its statutory responsibility to maintain the
adopted highway network. This could result in increased safety
risks for pedestrians and road users and reputational damage due to
service failure and public dissatisfaction. This option was not
recommended as it would lead to non-compliance with legal
obligations and have negative safety, financial and reputational
consequences.
 
Resolved that delegated authority is
given to the Executive Director of Place, in consultation with the
Executive Director of Finance and Transformation and Service
Director for Governance (Monitoring Officer) to conduct a compliant
procurement process in accordance with the Procurement Act 2023,
the Procurement Regulations 2024, and the Council’s Contract
Procedure Rules, and award the contract(s) to the most economically
advantageous tender(s).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to conduct an open procurement exercise to appoint suppliers for highway maintenance materials.

purpose:
This is a plan of Sandwell Local Authority's
Best Start in Life offer.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
Early
childhood development was a key determinant of long?term outcomes
in education, health and employment. Sandwell continued to face
significant challenges, including inequalities in child
development, delays in speech and language, and variation in school
readiness at age five. Addressing these issues at the earliest
stage was critical to improving life chances and reducing future
demand on public services.
 
The
Best Start in Life Plan had been commissioned by the Department for
Education as part of a national programme and provided a
coordinated, whole?system response developed with partners across
education, health, early help and the voluntary sector. It
established a shared strategic framework focused on improving
outcomes from pregnancy through to age five.
 
Delivery would be achieved through existing services and
partnerships, aligned around these priorities to provide a more
coherent and effective system of support.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Do nothing. This option would not meet the expectations
of the Department for Education national programme and would fail
to address identified local challenges relating to school
readiness, inequality and early child development. It would also
risk fragmentation of services and continued inefficiencies in
delivery. This option was therefore not recommended.
 
Option
2 – Develop a standalone service-based response. This option
would involve individual services responding independently to early
years challenges without an overarching framework. Whilst this may
deliver limited improvements within specific services, it would not
achieve the system?wide integration and consistency required to
address the scale and complexity of need across Sandwell. This
option was therefore not recommended.
 
Resolved that approval is given for
the Sandwell Best Start in Life Plan.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Sandwell Best Start in Life Plan to improve early childhood development outcomes

purpose:
The strategy sets out a clear, evidence-based
approach to ensuring sufficient, high-quality education provision
for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and
Disabilities (SEND). It responds to increasing demand for
Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), insufficient local
specialist provision, and the growing reliance on out-of-borough
placements
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
Local Authority had a statutory duty under s.14 of the Education
Act 1996 to ensure sufficient school places, including appropriate
provision for children with SEND.
 
This
duty was further reinforced through the Children and Families Act
2014 and the SEND Code of Practice (2014)
 
The
strategy responded to several interrelated challenges, including
rising numbers of Education, Health and Care Plans, increasing
complexity of need, insufficient specialist capacity within the
borough and a continued reliance on high?cost independent and
out?of?area placements. These pressures contributed to significant
financial challenges within the High Needs Block and impacting the
Council’s ability to deliver sustainable provision. The
proposed approach would support the development of additional local
specialist capacity, strengthen inclusion within mainstream
settings, enable more sustainable use of public resources and
improve outcomes for children and young people with
SEND.
 
The
strategy also operationalised national reforms by embedding
consistent commissioning standards, transparent placement pathways,
and equitable access across the borough.
 
The
Council was working with Newton Europe as its SEND transformation
partner to support delivery of a sustainable and high?quality SEND
system. This partnership strengthens the Council’s strategic
planning, demand forecasting and service design capability,
enabling a more coordinated approach across education, health and
care and ensuring that resources are directed effectively to meet
increasing levels of need.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Do nothing. This option would not enable the Council to
meet its statutory duties in relation to SEND sufficiency and would
result in continued growth in demand for high?cost out?of?borough
placements. It would also fail to respond to national policy
direction and improvement expectations. This option was therefore
not recommended.
 
Option
2 – Implement a partial or incremental approach. This option
would involve delivering elements of the strategy in a limited or
phased way without full system transformation. Whilst this may
provide some short?term improvement, it would not address the scale
of demand, would limit the ability to achieve financial
sustainability and would not deliver the level of change required
across the SEND system. This option was therefore not
recommended.
 
Resolved that approval is given for
the SEND Sufficiency Strategy 2026–2029, to allow for a
strategic approach to improving SEND sufficiency, including the
development of local specialist provision and strengthened
mainstream inclusion.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the SEND Sufficiency Strategy 2026-2029 to improve provision for children with SEND and strengthen inclusion in mainstream settings.

purpose:
To consider the Regeneration Pipeline
Performance.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
On the
23 March 2022, Cabinet approved the Regeneration Strategy,
Regeneration Project Pipeline, setting out the corporate
regeneration priorities for the period 2022 to 2027. The pipeline
was a live document, and Cabinet resolved for it to be monitored
via a report submitted to Cabinet every 6 months. The last report
was considered on the 10 December 2025.
 
In
addition, Cabinet resolved to approve additions to the project
pipeline and for the updated pipeline to be published on the
Council website and the Regenerating Sandwell website.
 
The
Council, as Accountable Body, was required to establish governance
and reporting arrangements to ensure the efficient award of grant
funding within the timescales agreed for each Partnership Board
Grant Funding programme.
 
The
Regeneration project pipeline comprised 61 live projects, in
addition to 26 projects that were now complete, bringing the
estimated total investment value to £3bn by 2027 and total
number of projects to 87.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1: Do Nothing (No change to the Regeneration Pipeline). The Council
could choose not to review or update the Regeneration Pipeline and
continue with existing arrangements without formal monitoring or
reporting. This option was not recommended as it would limit
transparency, reduce oversight of programme performance and risk
progress not being effectively scrutinised by Cabinet.
 
Option
2: Do not approve additional programmes within the pipeline. The
Council could choose not to include the Pride in Place programme
within the Regeneration Pipeline. This would result in fragmented
reporting and governance arrangements, limiting the Council’s
ability to maintain a comprehensive overview of regeneration
activity and potentially weakening strategic alignment across
programmes. This option was not recommended.
 
Option
3: To refuse the delegation of powers to the Smethwick, Friar Park
and Tividale Partnership Boards for administration and award of
grant funding for Pride in Place grant funded programmes. Key
operational and financial decisions would require repeated
Executive or Cabinet approvals. Given the scale and pace required
for Pride in Place delivery this approach was unworkable in
practice. It would create unnecessary bottlenecks, slow down
implementation, risk missing government deadlines, and compromise
the Council’s role as Accountable Body. This option was not
recommended.
 
Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that Cabinet receive and endorse the performance and
progress of the Regeneration Pipeline;
 
 

(2) 
that approval is given for the inclusion of the
Pride in Place programmes for Smethwick, Friar Park and Tividale in
future Regeneration Pipeline Performance reports to
Cabinet;
 

(3) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director – Place, in consultation with the Section 151
Officer and Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Economic Growth, to
progress the establishment of governance arrangements for the Pride
in Place Neighbourhood Board for Tividale and the preparation and
submission of Regeneration Plans, in accordance with Government
requirements and within approved governance frameworks;
 

(4) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director – Place in consultation with the Tividale
Neighbourhood Board, to submit a revised investment boundary to
government for approval;
 

(5) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director of to administer and distribute Pride in Place funding for
Smethwick, Friar Park and Tividale areas to the Smethwick
Partnership Board, Friar Park Partnership Board and Tividale
Partnership Board respectively on condition that reports on the
administration of the schemes are included within future
Regeneration Pipeline Performance reports to Cabinet;
 

(6) 
that Cabinet acknowledged that each Town Partnership
Board may award grant funding of up to £20million for each
relevant Pride in Place funding scheme.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Regeneration Strategy and Project Pipeline, with delegated authority for funding administration and distribution.

purpose:
Approve capital allocation for school building
works. The Schools Capital Programme is aligned to service needs
and enables the council to meet its statutory duty to ensure every
child in Sandwell has access to a good school place. The programme
supports this by prioritising the expansion of successful and
popular schools.
content:
Reasons for Recommendations
The
Council was facing a significant and growing demand for specialist
SEND provision. The number of Education, Health and Care Plans
(EHCPs) had risen to 5,156 as of June 2025 and could reach around
11,000 by 2030/31 if demand continued unchecked. This had increased
pressure on local services and led to greater reliance on expensive
independent and out-of-area placements.
 
To
address this, the Council proposed to expand local specialist
provision, including special schools and specialist inclusion
bases, so that more children and young people could be educated
within their own communities. These proposals supported the
Council’s SEND Sufficiency Strategy, aligned with national
SEND reforms and the Every Child
Achieving and Thriving White Paper (2026), and aim to reduce
pressure on the Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs
Block.
 
As
part of future planning, schools would be invited to submit
Expressions of Interest to host specialist inclusion bases. Any
proposals would be assessed against local need and suitability,
followed by detailed feasibility studies to determine whether
school buildings can support the required specialist
facilities.
 
Funding for feasibility studies was considered essential before
committing capital investment. These investigations would assess
building condition, accessibility, safety, capacity, costs, and
compliance requirements, ensuring that projects were practical,
affordable, and provide value for money. This work would help avoid
investment in unsuitable or undeliverable schemes and support
future decisions on SEND provision and School Condition Allocation
(SCA) funding.
 
Specific projects included:
 

·      
Grace Mary Primary School – Reconfiguration of
the existing specialist base and relocation of the nursery to
create improved specialist accommodation, increasing the school's
ability to support pupils with additional needs.

·      
King George V Primary School – Restoration of
a vacant Grade II listed former site manager’s house using a
£150,000 Department for Education grant to provide nursery
accommodation. The existing nursery space would then be converted
into a specialist base for pupils with SEND.
 
Any
procurement activities required to enable the delivery of the
programme would be undertaken in accordance with applicable
procurement legislation from time to time in force including but
not limited to the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 and
Procurement Act 2023 and required compliance with the
Council’s Procurement and Contract Procedure Rules
 

Alternative Options Considered
Feasibility studies for SEND provision and school condition
works
 
Do
nothing was rejected because capital funding was limited and
subject to strict regulations. Without feasibility studies, the
Council would risk poor investment decisions, financial and audit
issues, and non-compliance with funding requirements.
 
Proceed without feasibility studies was also rejected, as
projects could later prove to be unsuitable, unaffordable,
non-compliant with SEND or building safety standards, or unable to
meet future demand.
 
King
George V Primary School – Former Site Manager's
House
 
Do
nothing was rejected because the vacant listed building would
continue to deteriorate, creating safety risks, higher future
repair costs, and negative impacts on the local area. Demolition
was not a viable option due to its listed status.
 
Increase capacity within existing school buildings was rejected
because the school was already at full capacity. Using the former
house as a specialist base would also be less desirable than using
it for nursery provision, as specialist support should be
integrated within the main school wherever possible.
 
Grace
Mary Primary School – Nursery Relocation and Inclusion Base
Expansion
 
Do
nothing was rejected because the current accommodation is not
suitable for pupils with EHCPs and cannot be expanded to meet
growing demand, limiting the availability of appropriate SEND
places.
 
Use an
alternative site was not possible, as no suitable alternative
locations have been identified pending the outcome of feasibility
work.
 
Resolved:-
 

(1) 
that approval is given for the allocation of
£200,000 from the Council’s High Needs Capital
Allocation (HNCA) to fund feasibility work exploring potential
projects to increase the number of specialist bases places across
Sandwell. subject to a satisfactory financial appraisal being
approved by Strategic Finance for the programme and individual
component schemes;
 

(2) 
that approval is given for the allocation of
£200,000 from the School Condition Allocation (SCA) to
undertake feasibility work for schools not included in the School
Repair Account, enabling the investigation and preparation of
projects required to maintain and improve the school estate,
subject to a satisfactory financial appraisal being approved by
Strategic Finance for the programme and individual component
schemes;
 

(3) 
that approval is given the allocation of £1.9m
from the Council’s High Needs Capital Allocation to fund the
relocation of the nursery and expansion of the specialist base at
Grace Mary Primary School, subject to a satisfactory financial
appraisal being approved by Strategic Finance for the programme and
individual component schemes;
 

(4) 
that approval is given for the allocation of
£200,000 from the School Condition Allocation and
£50,000 from the High Needs Capital Allocation to support
refurbishment of the former site manager’s house at King
George V Primary School, subject to a satisfactory financial
appraisal being approved by Strategic Finance for the programme and
individual component schemes.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to allocate funds for feasibility studies and projects to address the growing demand for specialist SEND provision in Sandwell.

purpose:
Cabinet approval is required for the Tenant
Engagement Strategy.
content:
Approval was sought for the Tenant Engagement Strategy. Sandwell
was committed to putting tenants at the heart of the housing
service. The Council recognised that tenants, leaseholders, and
residents were key partners in shaping how the housing services
were delivered and improved. The housing stock comprised of over
27,700 homes across Sandwell—including low- and high-rise
flats, houses, bungalows, and maisonettes—serving a diverse
community. The Council wanted every tenant, regardless of
background or location, to feel heard, respected, and
supported.
 

Reason for Decision
Our
Tenant Engagement Strategy set out how the Council would listen to,
involve, and work alongside tenants to shape the homes and
communities where they live. It provided a clear framework for
partnership working, designed to empower tenants, enhance
satisfaction, and build trust. This meant providing meaningful
opportunities for residents to influence decisions, improve
services, and contribute to community wellbeing.
 
The
key aims of the Strategy was to:

·      
strengthen the tenant voice in decision-making and
service design;

·      
improve communication and transparency across all
housing services;

·      
make it easy and accessible for everyone to get
involved;

·      
promote accountability through regular feedback and
performance monitoring;

·      
build trust and stronger partnerships between
tenants and the council;

·      
ensure engagement is inclusive and reaches
underrepresented communities; and

·      
use tenant feedback and lived experiences to shape
continuous improvement.
 

Alternative Options Considered
An
alternative approach would be not to adopt the Tenant Engagement
Strategy. However, without this strategy in place, the council
would be unable to fully deliver the objectives of the Housing
Strategy 2023–2028, the Asset Management Strategy
2024–2029, Resident Engagement Strategies and the Regulatory
Housing Standards introduced in April 2024. Tenant engagement is
fundamental to meeting these requirements and ensuring services are
responsive, transparent, and accountable. Failure to adopt the
strategy would therefore lead to weaker governance, reduced tenant
influence, and less effective management of housing
services.
 
Resolved that the Tenant Engagement
Strategy is approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Tenant Engagement Strategy in Sandwell, prioritizing tenant involvement and satisfaction in housing services.

purpose:
Following the Examination in Public of the
Sandwell Local Plan the council and the inspector have identified a
number of modifications to resolve soundness and legal compliance
issues.
content:
Approval was sought for the list of main modifications,
amendments to plan diagrams and plans within the Sandwell Local
Plan which would be circulated for public consultation. It was a
statutory requirement of every Local Planning Authority to have an
up-to-date Local Plan. The revised National Planning Policy
Framework (NPPF), released in December 2024, contained transitional
arrangements that required local planning authorities to submit
local plans by March 2025 for them to be considered under the
previous NPPF (2023) and regulations. The Sandwell’s Local
Plan was submitted to the Secretary of State in December
2024.
 
The
timetable for producing the Plan was set out in the Local
Development Scheme (LDS), the latest version of which was approved
by Cabinet on 05 February 2025 and which
was published on the Council’s website. The LDS set out the
timetable for the current Draft Sandwell Local Plan as well as an
indicative timetable for reviewing the Plan under the new NPPF and
regulations. The LDS would be reviewed early 2026.
 

Reason for Decision
The
Examination in Public of the Draft Plan commenced when the Council
submitted the Draft Plan to the Secretary of State via the Planning
Inspectorate. A Planning Inspector had then been appointed to
examine the Draft Plan.
 
The
Inspector had identified a number of
Matters, Issues and Questions (MIQs) for the Draft Plan which had
been discussed with the Council and other representors at public
hearing sessions held during the weeks commencing 14 July 2025, 22
September and 29 September 2025. Other respondents included West
Midlands Police, the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust,
Friends of Sheepwash Urban Park and
Sport England, along with planning consultants acting on behalf of
private clients with housing allocations in the plan.
 
Following the hearing sessions, the Inspector suggested
a number of main modifications that
would resolve any legal compliance issues for the DSLP. These
modifications ranged in scope from redrafting parts of an
individual policy or reasoned justification to the deletion or
amalgamation of whole policies and rearranging the format of the
document. There were also proposed changes to the Policies Map,
which was the geographical representation of the policies in the
SLP.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Consult on the proposed main modifications to comply with
legislative requirements to allow adoption of a Local
Plan.
The
Planning Inspector was likely to recommend that the plan as
submitted (without the main modifications) should not be adopted,
before recommending main modifications to make the submitted plan
legally compliant. The Town and Country Planning (Local
Planning)(England) Regulations 2012
required the Council to consult on any main modifications to the
Local Plan before incorporating them into the Local
Plan.
 
Section 20 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act required
that the Council should then make the recommended main
modifications, together with any additional modifications at their
discretion, if they wished to adopt the plan. The Council would not
be able to adopt the Sandwell Local Plan if the main modifications
were not made to it. Therefore, there was no other option but to
consult on the main modifications if the Council wished to adopt
the Draft Plan.
 

Resolved:-

(1)          
that approval is given to the list of main
modifications, amendments to plan diagrams and plans within the
Sandwell Local Plan for public consultation, to commence on 16
February 2026 for a period of 6 weeks to 30 March 2026;

 

(2)          
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director for Place, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Housing and Planning:
 

a)            
to agree any necessary amendments to supporting
documentation for consultation and any other typographical,
presentational, and consequential wording changes to the Local Plan
prior to publication;

 

b)            
following public consultation on the Proposed Main
Modifications, consider and summarise the responses received and
forward to the Inspectors for their consideration in producing
their Report. That following the receipt of the Report from the
Inspector recommending adoption of the Local Plan, that the Plan be
brought back to Cabinet and Full Council for adoption.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve main modifications and amendments to the Sandwell Local Plan for public consultation.

purpose:
To consider the Safer Neighbourhoods and
Active Communities Scrutiny Board Scrutiny Review
Recommendations.
content:
Consideration was given to the recommendations of Safer
Neighbourhoods and Active Communities Scrutiny Board in respect of
the Scrutiny Review of the Communities in our Borough.
 
The
Safer Neighbourhoods and Active Communities Scrutiny Board
commenced the Scrutiny Review of the Communities in our Borough in
the 2023/ 24 municipal year.
 
The
Board established a working group to conduct the review which
undertook substantial research and efforts to understand the matter
and produce recommendations to the Executive.
 
At the
meeting of the Safer neighbourhoods and Active Communities Scrutiny
Board in January 2026 the Board agreed range of recommendations
based on the research and findings of the working group. These
recommendations are now presented to Cabinet for
consideration.
 

Reason for Decision
There
was a strong evidence base demonstrating that cohesive,
well?connected
communities experience better outcomes across health, safety,
education, and economic participation. Following the 2024 riots,
members identified a need to examine how Sandwell could strengthen
cohesion, improve communication, and support residents to feel part
of their local area.
 
The
review sought to understand these issues through a combination of
quantitative data, qualitative engagement, site visits, and
comparative research.
 
Through the evidence gathered, members found that cohesion was
strengthened when residents can communicate effectively with
services, when trusted messengers help bridge gaps in engagement,
and when local assets were visible, accessible and easy to
navigate. Opportunities for communities to mix, celebrate and
collaborate also play a vital role, as did ensuring that
information was clear, consistent and available in multiple
languages.
 

Alternative Options Considered
There
were no alternative options to consider.
 

Resolved:-

(1) 
that approval is given in full to the
recommendations of Safer Neighbourhoods and Active Communities
Scrutiny Board in respect of the Scrutiny Review of the Communities
in our Borough as follows:-
 
a)   
that the Cabinet Member for Business and Skills
create a publicly accessible comprehensive directory of English for
Speakers of Other Languages courses;
 
b)   
that the Statutory Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member
for Finances and Resources conduct a coordinated campaign to
increase the profile and awareness of English for Speakers of Other
Languages courses across the borough;
 
c)   
that the Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for
Communities and Neighbourhoods produce and develop a borough wide
Community Asset Map of organisations, services, and resources by
ward
 
 

(2) 
that approval is given in part to the recommendation
of Safer Neighbourhoods and Active Communities Scrutiny Board in
respect of the Scrutiny Review of the Communities in our Borough as
follows:-
 
a)   
that the Deputy Leader of the Council and Cabinet
Member for Communities and Neighbourhoods promote and support
inclusive community events and cultural celebration days in public
spaces, with family friendly activities provided free of
charge.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations from the Safer Neighbourhoods and Active Communities Scrutiny Board regarding the Scrutiny Review of the Communities in the Borough.

Approval was sought to delegate powers to the Black Country
Joint Executive Committee to approve major transport schemes, which

authorities of Sandwell, Dudley, Walsall, and Wolverhampton, to
allow for collective decision-making and coordination on major
infrastructure investment, support regional connectivity, growth,
and efficient governance across the Black Country.
 

Reason for Decision
The
four Black Country Councils collaborated extensively on regional
transport and infrastructure matters through the Black Country
Transport Officers Group and the West Midlands Combined Authority
(WMCA) frameworks. There was currently no single governance body
with delegated authority to take joint executive decisions on
transport infrastructure projects of shared
significance.
 
The
lack of regional delegation arrangements for transport projects
required decisions to be taken by each Executive whose Local
Authority was involved in the transport project concerned. Major
transport projects by their nature, often covered two or more local
authority areas. If a scheme required approval at each key stage by
each of the four Black Country Authorities, this would require
sixteen separate approvals across four key project
stages.
Furthermore, the calendars for meetings of the Executive rarely
aligned, meaning a potential delay of more than two months while
awaiting all Executives to make the necessary
resolutions.
 
Delegating decision making to the formal Joint Committee would
streamline approvals, enhance accountability, and ensure consistent
decision-making while retaining local democratic
oversight.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1: Maintain existing arrangements. This option would not deliver
efficient strategic transport decision-making and would limit the
effective co-ordination of the delivery of key strategic highways
and transport infrastructure schemes within the Black Country. This
option was dismissed.
 
Option
2: Create a non-decision-making joint committee. This option would
not deliver efficiencies in strategic transport decision-making and
limit the effective co-ordination of the delivery of key strategic
highways and transport infrastructure schemes within the Black
Country. This option was dismissed.
 

Resolved:-

(1)          
that delegated authority is given to the Black
Country Joint Executive Committee to allow for approval and
delivery of transport and highways infrastructure schemes that fall
within the Council’s executive functions and are identified
as strategic Black Country infrastructure priorities;

 

(2)          
that approval is given to amended the Terms of Reference for the Black Country
Joint Executive Committee set out at Appendix 1;

 

(3)          
that delegated authority is given to the Monitoring
Officer and Service Director of Governance to make any necessary
and consequential changes to Part 2.3: Responsibilities for
Functions in the Constitution and to finalise these in consultation
with the other Black Country authorities for inclusion within the
Constitutions of each authority;

 

(4)          
that approval is given so that existing scrutiny
arrangements for decisions of the Black Country Joint Executive
Committee be retained and be undertaken by each Council’s
relevant Scrutiny Committee/Board;

 

(5)          
that delegated authority is given to the Monitoring
Officer and Service Director of Governance to make any
consequential constitutional or procedural amendments required to
give effect to these arrangements.
topline: The Black Country Council has decided to delegate powers to the Joint Executive Committee for approving major transport schemes.

purpose:
To consider the Medium-Term Financial Strategy
and Draft Budget 2026/27.
content:
The
Council had a track record of sound financial management and
control. This had continued in 2025/26. The budget included
£20m of income and expenditure changes and these were
achieving high levels of success. Any emerging issues had been
identified quickly and mitigated. Performance was published via
reports to senior leadership and the Cabinet, and with ongoing
reporting to the Council’s Scrutiny Boards. This activity had
meant that, at quarter two, the Council was forecasting an
underspend within the revenue General Fund.
 
The
Council continued to report positive achievements against the
strategic aims of the Council Plan. This had included the
announcement of a ‘Good’ rating from OFSTED for
Children’s Services and the
Council was a finalist in the LGA Awards category for Most Improved
Council. Such evidence indicated a positive direction of travel in
relation to the assessment of value for money.
 

Reason for Decision
The
Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) showed how the Council could
deploy resources to achieve its strategic objectives, as set out in
the Council Plan. It showed how expenditure and income budgets
change to ensure services were adequate to address local need and
meet financial pressures from inflation and increasing
demand.
 
The
immediate objective of the updated MTFS was focused on achieving a
balanced budget for 2026/27, but the principal aim was to provide a
comprehensive, forward-looking framework over the MTFS period that
ensured long-term financial sustainability, allowing the Council to
deliver its key strategic priorities and statutory services within
a balanced budget in future years.
 

Alternative Options Considered
The
Council was legally required to set a balanced budget by March each
year. As such, there was no alternative other than to set a
balanced budget.
 

Resolved:-

that the Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Draft
Budget Report 2026/27, including the appendix and annexes set out
in Appendix A, is endorsed and recommended to Full Council for
approval, incorporating the following recommendations:

Annex 1;

Annex 2 for inclusion in the General Fund base budget for 2026/27
and the Medium-Term Financial Plan for the financial years 2026/27
to 2030/31;

proposals, detailed in Annex 3 for inclusion in the General Fund
base budget for 2026/27 and the Medium-Term Financial Plan
Medium-Term Financial Plan for the financial years 2026/27 to
2030/31;

 

d)

7;

ii)

iii)

iv)

and Recovery Improvement Grant (DATRIG) amount for the 2026/27

and harms and is to be additional to existing Public Health grant

content:
Approval was sought for the distribution of the Drug and Alcohol
Treatment and Recovery Improvement Grant for substance misuse
treatment and recovery and for Individual Placement and Support.
Sandwell’s had received the allocated Drug and Alcohol
Treatment and Recovery Improvement Grant budget for 2026/27, with
further indicative amounts for 2027/28 and 2028/29.
 

Reason for Decision
The
Drug and Alcohol Treatment and Recovery Improvement Grant /
Supplemental Substance Misuse Treatment Funding was governed by a
nationally defined Menu of Interventions produced by the Office for
Health Improvement and Disparities. Local authorities were required
to attribute every element of spend to one or more intervention
categories. The Menu of Interventions was structured to reflect the
10-Year Drug Strategy and system-wide aims to:

·      
Increase treatment capacity

·      
Reduce drug- and alcohol-related harm

·      
Improve recovery outcomes

·      
Strengthen the workforce

·      
Embed prevention and early intervention

·      
Strengthen criminal justice and community safety
links
 
The
funding was required to be spent on interventions that aim to
achieve the Drug Strategy ambition to reduce drug and alcohol
related deaths and harms and was to be additional to existing
Public Health grant expenditure on substance misuse treatment
services.
 
The
Strategy therefore required that local areas rebuild and reinvest
into local support systems towards “a world class drug
treatment and recovery system” Monies can only be spent on
provisions that fit within Office for Health Improvement and
Disparities Menu of Interventions.
 
It had
been announced that Sandwell would receive three further years of
funding for 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29. The funding was to be
additional to existing Public Health grant expenditure on substance
misuse treatment services.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Do not
approve distribution of the Drug and Alcohol Treatment and Recovery
Improvement Grant as required by Office for Health Improvement and
Disparities and not utilise the additional funding but simply
return the monies to government. This would mean that the local
treatment population would not benefit from the quality and
capacity improvements that the monies could afford.
 

Resolved:-

(1)          
that approval is given for the proposal for
distribution of the Drug and Alcohol Treatment and Recovery
Improvement Grant for substance misuse treatment and recovery and
for Individual Placement and Support (IPS). As required by Office
for Health Improvement and Disparities grant conditions;

 

(2)          
that approval is given for the years 2026/27,
2027/28 and 2028/29 based on the Indicative amount still subject to
Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) and Treasury approvals,
even though the final allocation could vary;

 

(3)          
that approval is given for the variation to the
current Adult Alcohol and Drug Service Contract to fund additional
enhanced provision for the period 2026/27, in line with cost
increases, and that delegated authority is given to the Director of
Public Health to approve the variation, in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Adult Services, Health and Wellbeing;

 

(4)          
that delegated authority is given to the Director of
Public Health to determine the distribution of the Drug and Alcohol
Treatment and Recovery Improvement Grant over the grant period
covering the financial year 2026/27, 27/28 and 28/209, in agreement
with Cabinet Member for Adult Services, Health and Wellbeing;

 

(5)          
that delegated authority is given to the Director of
Public Health, in consultation with the Service Director -
Governance and Monitoring Officer, to authorise variations to the
existing Adult Alcohol and Drug Service contract allowing the
additional enhanced provision for the remaining period of the
contract term which will end 31 January 2028;

 

(6)          
that delegated authority is given to the Director of
Public Health to award and enter into
any contract(s), on terms to be agreed by the Director of Public
Health, for the provision of services funded by the Drug and
Alcohol Treatment and Recovery Improvement Grant funds;
and

 

(7)          
that delegated authority is given to the Service
Director - Governance and Monitoring Officer to take any actions as
may be required to give effect to the proposals in these
recommendations for the provision of Drug and Alcohol Treatment and
Recovery Improvement Grant funded provisions.

purpose:
To consider the re-commissioning of Sandwell
Community Dementia Service.
content:
Approval was sought to commence a procurement exercise to
re-commission the Sandwell Community Dementia Service. Dementia was
a major contributor to long-term support needs. Community
post-diagnosis support improved
understanding, planning, carer resilience and connection to local
services. It supported system resilience by reducing avoidable
escalation to crisis responses and higher-cost care.
 

Reason for Decision
The
Sandwell Community Dementia Service provided a single point of
access and a tiered support offer delivered with Voluntary and
Community Sector partners. The contract expired on 28 September
2026 with no remaining extension options, requiring procurement to
maintain continuity.
 
On 18
December 2025, the Sandwell Joint Partnership Board considered the
future commissioning arrangements for the service and agreed that
recommissioning should proceed within the existing Better Care Fund
allocation, subject to an inflationary uplift, which for the
present time would be estimated at 5%.
 
The
estimated costs for the first year of the new contract would be
£416,948. Over a three year period
and assuming a 5% annual uplift each year, this would equate to a
contract value of £1,314,428.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Do nothing: allowing the contract to expire would remove
a key element of the dementia pathway and was rejected due to the
significant impact on residents and partner
organisations.
 
Option
2 – Recommission with growth funding: this option was
considered but not approved by the Joint Partnership Board due to
affordability concerns.
 

Resolved:-

(1)          
that approval is given for the recommissioning of
the Sandwell Community Dementia Service through a competitive
procurement process for a period of three years with the option to
extend for up to a further two years;

 

(2)          
that approval is given that the service will operate
within the existing Better Care Fund budget subject only to annual
inflationary uplifts;

 

(3)          
that approval is given for the inclusion of a
contract modification provision, in accordance with the Procurement
Act 2023, to allow for a cumulative increase of up to 50% of the
initial contract value, where required to address a known and
evidenced risk relating to sustained increases in demand that
cannot be safely or effectively managed within the original
contract value;

 

(4)          
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director – Adult Social Care and Health, in consultation with
the Cabinet Member for Adult Services, Health and Well-being, to
approve the final service specification and award the contract;
and

 

(5)          
that approval is given for an exemption to rule 8.7
of Procurement and Contract Procedure Rules 2018-19, or subsequent
amendment, to allow the Executive Director – Adult Social
Care and Health to award contracts to the successful tenderer(s) if
the required minimum number of tenders are not received.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to recommission the Sandwell Community Dementia Service through a competitive procurement process for a period of three years.

purpose:

content:
Approval was sought to publish the Local Authority’s
Admission Arrangements for 2027/28 academic year for places in all
community and voluntary controlled schools in accordance with the
School Admissions Code 2021.
 

Reason for Decision
The
Council was required to abide by the requirements of the School
Admissions Code and associated regulations and determine admission
arrangements for community and voluntary controlled schools each
year. The proposed determined arrangements were in line with the
requirements of the Admissions Code.
 
The
Admissions Code published in September 2021 required the Council,
to formally agree admission arrangements for those schools every
year, even if the arrangements had not changed from previous years.
Admission authorities were required to determine admission
arrangements for entry in September 2027 by 28 February
2026.
 

Alternative Options Considered
No
other options had been considered. The Council was legally required
to determine the admission arrangements for community and voluntary
controlled schools, to determine a co-ordinated scheme which
explained the co-ordination of arrangements for all publicly funded
schools in the Sandwell area, and to consult as
appropriate.
 
Resolved that delegated authority is
given to the Executive Director of Children and Education to
publish the Local Authority’s Admission Arrangements for
2027/28 academic year for places in all community and voluntary
controlled schools, in accordance with the School Admissions Code
2021.
