purpose:
Procurement of integrated housing systems to
meet regulatory and organisational requirements
content:
Approval was sought
for procurement and award a contract for a new Integrated Housing
Management software solution. The new software solution once in
place would allow the Council as a regulated provider of social
housing, to satisfy the requirements of Regulator of Social
Housing  and resolve operational
limitations in existing systems.
 

Reason for Decision
The Building Safety
Regulator (BSR) and the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) had made
significant changes to the way landlords were required to build,
manage and maintain properties, engage with tenants, maintain
digital records, and report compliance and performance.
 
As a landlord, a
failure by the Council to comply with the BSR was a criminal
offence and the Council risked enforcement. Non-compliance with
these landlord requirements was an offence. Responsibility sat with
individual officers and a newly created concept of the
‘Accountable Persons’ who would assume responsibility
for the safety of high-rise buildings.
 
As a registered
provider of social housing, the Council was required to establish
the systems, data accuracy, and the effective and efficient
processes needed to ensure compliance with these regulatory
requirements.
 
It was not currently
possible for the Council to be fully compliant with the regulatory
framework, without having comprehensive asset management and
compliance management systems, and high-quality up-to-date stock
condition data. Integrated Housing Management System procurement
sought to address system gaps and weaknesses.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option 1 –
Continue with existing systems. Consideration was given to
continuing to operate with existing systems. This was discounted
for several reasons, including:
·     
Lagacy Housing Management System (reaching end of life)
·     
Lack of a Compliance Management System (commitment to RSH to
procure and implement)
·     
Lack of an Asset Management System (commitment to RSH to Procure
and implement)
·     
Legacy Repairs Management System (opportunity to consider as an
integrated part of IHMS, rather than a standalone system)
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that delegated authority is given to the Executive Director for
Place in consultation with, the Executive Director for Finance and
Transformation and the Service Director – Governance
(Monitoring Officer) and the Cabinet Member for Housing to
undertake an appropriate competitive procurement exercise for the
provision of an Integrated Housing Management System;

 
(2)         
that delegated authority is given to the Service Director –
Governance (Monitoring Officer) in consultation with the Executive
Director for Place and the Executive Director for Finance and
Transformation to prepare and publish all necessary procurement and
tender documentation under the Competitive Flexible Procedure under
the Procurement Act 2023;

 
(3)         
that a further report is submitted on conclusion of the procurement
exercise setting out the evaluation of tenders and making
recommendations for the award of contract.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the procurement and award of a contract for a new Integrated Housing Management software solution to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements for social housing providers.

purpose:
The West Midlands Safe Centre (WMSC) aims to
provide secure care for vulnerable young people with complex needs,
offering trauma-informed and integrated health and education
services.
content:
Approval was sought
to progress the West Midlands Safe Centre project, including the
proposed establishment of the most appropriate legal form of
Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to enable the construction and
operation of the West Midlands Safe Centre on behalf of the West
Midlands local authorities for public sector delivery of secure
children services. Once delivered the Safe Centre would be the
first regionally owned secure children’s home in the country,
providing 20 secure welfare beds and high-quality care, health and
education to local children, saving local authorities, including
Sandwell, from high-cost private care placements and reducing the
use and cost of unregulated provision.
 

Reason for Decision
Secure
children’s homes were safe settings for children whose
liberty was restricted, where they could be supported through
trauma aware and psychologically informed integrated care, health
and educational services. Secure children’s homes supported
highly vulnerable young people with complex needs, providing care,
health, and education in a safe environment where their liberty was
restricted. These children often faced multiple placement
breakdowns, missed education, unresolved emotional and physical
health issues, and significant trauma.
 
There was a national
shortage of secure placements for these vulnerable children, as
highlighted by Ofsted, with 50 children waiting for a secure
welfare placement on any given day. A total of 15 Sandwell children
were placed in secure welfare during the period 2019–2025
with several other children in unregulated provision due to lack of
availability of secure welfare. The West Midlands had no dedicated
regional provision creating pressure on the existing secure
estate.
 
The West Midlands
Safe Centre would be the first regionally owned secure
children’s home in the country, providing 20 secure welfare
beds and high-quality care, health and education to local children,
saving local authorities, including Sandwell, from high-cost
private care placements and reducing the use and cost of
unregulated provision.
 
Sandwell
Children’s Trust was responsible for delivering
children’s social care services and securing appropriate
placements for the children we care for. Operating under the
governance and oversight of Sandwell Council, the Trust worked in
partnership with the local authority to ensure that vulnerable
children and young people receive the support, protection, and care
they need.
 
12 of the 14 West
Midlands local authorities, (including Birmingham and Sandwell
Children’s Trusts), were currently committed in principle to
joining and authorities involved would be taking a formal decision
to progress this provision through their governance process from
September – December 2025.
 
The set up of the
West Midlands Safe Centre was entirely funded by the Department for
Education (DfE) who had recognised the national shortage of secure
welfare beds and the lack of provision within the West Midlands
region. The DfE capital funding of £61.8m for construction
and “Seed Funding” revenue grant of up to £8.4m
had been secured.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option 1 - Do nothing
– This would not resolve the shortage of secure welfare care
for the most vulnerable children in the West Midlands. Local
authorities would continue to have to place vulnerable children at
a significant distance from their local areas, away from their
families and other networks. This option was therefore not
recommended.
 
Option 2 - Proceed
with the project and establish a structured SPV as a Company
Limited by Guarantee (CLG) – Whilst this scored favourably in
the options appraisal, tax advice identified a potential VAT and
corporation tax liability with a CLG. Whilst a CLG could seek tax
exemptions, there would be no guarantee of this and there would be
a risk of delay in securing HMRC confirmations or approvals, which
could affect operational timelines, especially if the CLG was to
act as an SPV for public service delivery, so this option was not
considered beneficial at the writing of this report and may need to
be revisited and reported by to the West Midlands Safe Centre
Project Board for consideration.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that subject to the completion of the legal due diligence work, the
development of the West Midlands Safe Centre as set out in the
business case that has been submitted to the Department for
Education is endorsed;

 
(2)         
that the proposed legal formation of a Special Purpose Vehicle,
subject to the completion of the legal due diligence work is
endorsed:
 
(3)         
that approval is given to the arrangements for the Council to join
the Special Purpose Vehicle and be part of a formal partnership for
governance of the West midlands Safe Centre with other West
Midlands local authorities with a share proportion as set out in
the report;

 
(4)         
that further reports be submitted for Cabinet approval prior to any
action continuing the Council’s participation in the
Partnership Agreement at a revised share if insufficient local
authority members sign up and the maximum Sandwell share of 8.83%
is exceeded;
 
(5)         
that approval is given in principle the proposed procurement
approach and property arrangements for the operation of the West
Midlands Safe Centre asset out in this report and supporting
appendices;
 
(6)         
that delegated authority is given to the Executive Director of
Children and Education Services in conjunction with the Executive
Director of Finance and Transformation (S.151 officer) and Service
Director for Governance / Monitoring Officer (or their delegates),
to undertake the following:
 
(a)         
complete the necessary due diligence required including but not
limited to legal and tax due diligence arrangements; and
(b)         
thereafter to complete all necessary documents to give effect to
the above recommendations. The delegation shall also include the
power to do anything necessary, incidental or ancillary for the
carrying into effect the recommendations set out in this
report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to progress the West Midlands Safe Centre project to provide secure children services.

purpose:
To consider the Provision of Mortuary and
Pathology Services for the Black Country Coroners
Service.
content:
Approval was sought for the Provision of
Mortuary and Pathology Services for the Black Country Coroners
Service. As the relevant authority for the Black Country Coroners
service, Sandwell had an obligation to put in place the necessary
resources to enable the Coroner to
discharge their judicial responsibilities which included the
provision of mortuary and pathology services.
 

Reason for Decision
A
formal collaborative agreement was in place with the other Black
Country Local Authorities. The agreement set out that expenditure
was shared equally between the four authorities with two
exceptions, one being mortuary and pathology services and the
second, removals on behalf of the coroner. Where costs were shared
equally Sandwell Council administered and managed the contract
arrangements of all expenditure for the services provided to the
coroner. Expenditure was then recharged on a quarterly basis to
each of the Black Country local authorities.
 

Alternative Options Considered
The
coroner’s judicial role and responsibilities were outlined by
the Coroners and Justice Act 2009 and for expenditure, Coroners
Allowances, Fees and Expenses Regulations 2013. These provisions
required access to post-mortem examinations to help determine cause
of death.
 
Given
the statutory duty place upon the Council as the relevant
authority, Sandwell was required ensure uninterrupted access to
mortuary and pathology services and therefore a contract must be in
place, with no alternative options reasonably available.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director for Finance and Transformation to undertake a procurement
exercise for the delivery of a mortuary and pathology provision for
the Black Country Coroner for a contract term of four years (1
April 2026 to 31 March 2030);

 
(2) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director for Finance and Transformation in consultation with the
Service Director Governance and Monitoring Officer to award and
enter into agreements with all successful bidders for the provision
of mortuary and pathology services, for the Black Country Coroner
for a contract term of four years (1 April 2026 to 31 March
2030);
 
(3) 
that delegated authority is given to the Service
Director Governance and Monitoring Officer, or their designated
representative, to execute any documents necessary within a
reasonable time to give effect to the proposal in recommendation
(2) above for the provision of mortuary and pathology services;
 
(4) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director for Finance and Transformation in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources to apply, if necessary,
any exemptions that need to be made to the Council’s Contract
Procedure Rules 2024, to allow for contracts to be awarded to the
successful tenderer(s) in relation to (2) above.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to procure mortuary and pathology services for the Black Country Coroners Service.

purpose:
Sandwell Council's EDI Strategy using the LGA
Equality Framework.
content:
Approval was sought for the EDI (Equality, Diversity and
inclusion) Strategy 2026-29. Under the Equality Act 2010, the
Council was legally required to ensure that equality was actively
considered and embedded throughout its services and functions. In
support of this, the Public Sector Equality Duty mandated that
local authorities assess the impact of decisions and services on
diverse communities, set and publish specific measurable equality
objectives at least every four years, publish equality data and
ensure that public services were responsive to the needs of all
population groups.
 
Association (LGA) Equality Framework (Appendix 3), which serves
as a valuable guide for the council’s ongoing improvement in
EDI. The framework is structured around four key thematic areas,
each supported by specific considerations:
 
·      
understanding and working with communities:
fostering meaningful engagement and insight into diverse community
needs;
·      
leadership and organisational commitment:
demonstrating strategic leadership and embedding EDI across all
levels of the organisation;
·      
responsive services and customer care: ensuring
services were inclusive, accessible, and tailored to meet varied
needs; and
·      
diverse and engaged workforce: promoting workforce
diversity and cultivating an inclusive workplace
culture.
 

Reason for Decision
The
EDI Strategy 2026-29 was closely aligned with the Local Government
Association (LGA) Equality Framework, which served as a valuable
guide for the Council’s ongoing improvement in EDI. The
proposed strategy reinforced the Council’s commitment to the
nine statutory protected characteristics, and also the locally
adopted characteristic of being care experienced. This framework
ensured that the Council had due regard to equality considerations
when designing services and implementing policy. The strategy set
out the roadmap to achieve excellent performance against the
Equality Framework for Local Government, which underpinned the
commitments made within the Council Plan 2024 –
2027.
 
The
adoption of the strategy would support the embedding of the
Council’s organisational values and behaviours. Staff were
expected to collaborate, support each other, put residents first,
celebrate diversity, strive for improvement, and deliver
high-quality services, fostering a positive, respectful workplace
culture. To embed these values and behaviours into daily practice,
robust objectives relating to EDI were needed which were detailed
in the strategy relating to improving our understanding and working
with our communities, our leadership and organisational commitment,
responsive services and customer care, and having a diverse and
engaged workforce.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Continue without an EDI Strategy. This was not recommended as
rejecting this proposal would dismantle the four strategic
priorities that underpin the approach to equality and remove the
specific LGA Equality Framework for embedding inclusion into the
Council’s everyday operations. Moreover, failure to approve
the strategy would place the Council in breach of its legal
obligation under the Equality Act 2010 to publish equality
objectives, which as per published objective in 2023 the Council
was committed to this strategy, leaving the Council non-compliant
and exposed to significant reputational and legal risk.
 
Resolved that approval is given to the
Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Strategy 2026–2029,
‘Unity through Inclusion’.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Strategy 2026-29, aligning with legal obligations and promoting equality and diversity within the council's operations.

purpose:
To seek approval from Cabinet to implement and
launch the council's digital strategy, and to seek strategic
commitment to its delivery.
content:
Approval was sought for the Sandwell Digital Strategy 2025-28.
The need for a digital strategy was driven by the need to establish
a clear, modern, strategy for digital delivery. Crucially, the
Strategy’s primary driver was addressing digital exclusion,
ensuring every resident had the skills, confidence, and access to
use the Council's established digital services, fulfilling the
Council’s commitment to an inclusive Sandwell. Achievement of
this continuous improvement and efficiency was essential in the
context of persistent financial challenges. Furthermore, rapid
advancements in technology, particularly in areas like automation,
data analytics, and cloud services, present transformative
opportunities that the Council’s existing framework was not
optimised to utilise.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the Strategy and emphasised how
increased use of technology and technological solutions such as
artificial intelligence could lead to innovation and improvements
across services.
 

Reason for Decision
The
current digital infrastructure and service model faced significant
pressures. Firstly, resident expectations had been reshaped by
private sector experiences and extensive use of the existing
portfolio of MySandwell 24/7 access to
online self-services. These established services had become
essential for customers and fundamental to the Council’s
operations, realising the rationalisation of human resources
through the efficient processing of hundreds of thousands of
customer transactions each year. The support and maintenance and
expansion of these services required continuous development to
realise its fuller potential. The Council’s current
operational framework for this expansion was insufficient and
unsustainable and required structured investment.
 
The
strategy ensured the Council maintained existing digital services
in compliance with evolving legislative standards, while
proactively investing in the Council’s internal digital
skills and transformation expertise to create and deliver projects
and programmes that achieve sustainable staff capacity creation and
operational streamlining. Maximising operational efficiency was
essential for the Council’s financial viability, standards of
customer experience and achievement of its wider
ambitions.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1: Maintain the Current State. This option involved rejecting the
Digital Strategy and continuing to operate with the existing
fragmented digital policies, legacy IT systems, and the current
pace of service digitisation. This decision would exacerbate the
risk of digital exclusion for residents and create a widening gap
between resident expectations and Council service
capability.
 
Option
2: Incremental, Service-by-Service Digital Improvements. This
option involved approving a policy to proceed with decentralised,
uncoordinated digital transformation projects managed independently
by individual service directorates. This approach risked creating
new "digital silos" where technologies and data platforms cannot
communicate effectively across the Council, hindering the "One
Council One Team" strategic theme. This option would ultimately
result in higher integration costs, duplicated effort, and a poor,
inconsistent experience for residents who interact with multiple
Council services.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1) 
that approval is given to the Sandwell Digital
Strategy 2025 – 2028;
 
(2) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director - Finance & Transformation, in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources, to finalise and implement
the detailed annual delivery plans required to execute the
Strategy.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Sandwell Digital Strategy 2025-28, aiming to address digital exclusion and improve digital services for residents.

content:
Approval was sought for SEND Transformation and the improvement
of SEND services. Over recent years, Sandwell had experienced a
significant rise in the number of Children and Young People (CYP)
with Educational Health and Care Plans (EHCP), reflecting both
national trends and increasing local demand for specialist
support.
 
Sandwell had seen a sharp and sustained rise in EHCPs with the
number of CYP supported by plans reaching 4,064 in January 2025 ,
an increase of 62% over five years. The rise underscored the
growing complexity of needs among pupils and the corresponding
pressure on local services to deliver timely and effective
provision.
 
The
vision for the SEND Transformation programme was to ensure that
every child and young person received support in the right place,
at the right time for as long as it is required, with educational
achievement and independent outcomes at the heart of any changes,
enabling improvement of outcomes, workforce practice, and financial
performance.
 
Cabinet Members agreed that it was imperative that those
children and young people with SEND were provided with the
necessary high quality support, and that services providing that
support were meeting their needs and building strong foundations
for adulthood.
 

Reason for Decision
The
council had established a SEND Transformation programme to achieve
its vision, whilst also aiming to address the risk of material
overspending within the High Needs Block of the Council's Dedicated
Schools Grant (DSG). The implementation and delivery of the
programme required additional capacity and specialist expertise
from a commissioned SEND Transformation Partner through a compliant
procurement process.
 
The
Council’s Corporate Risk Register, identified that if the
Council did not consider options on how to manage the increasing
upwards trajectory of demand in respect of SEND travel assistance
and both the demand and cost of SEND placements, then there would
be significant impact on the council’s budget and the DSG
High Needs Block.
 
A
specialist transformation partner would provide the proven
methodologies, experience, tools, and additional capacity to
progress transformation at pace, drawing on approaches that have
been successfully applied within the sector across other local
authorities.
 
The
transformation partner would work alongside an experienced
programme manager. The programme manager would be responsible for
co-ordinating the full SEND Transformation Programme and would have
full visibility of activities across the service, manage the
activity and outputs of the transformation partner, and work
alongside strategic managers reporting directly to the Executive
Director, Children and Education.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1- Do not appoint a transformation partner and utilise internal
resource to progress transformation activity. This option despite
appearing to be cost-effective was not feasible in the long-term
due to the current business as usual pressures, complexity of
transformation required, and capacity constraints across the
service. It did not sufficiently address the need for additional
capacity and specialist skills to deliver transformation at pace.
This approach saw risk of burnout and turnover of staff due to the
pressures of delivering business as usual, the Council’s
commitments to the Local Area Partnership, OFSTED, and the
Department of Education and transformation activity with limited
capacity. This option was therefore dismissed.
 
Option
2- Do not deliver further transformational activities (‘do
nothing’). Consideration had been given to the option of
maintaining the current position without initiating further
transformation activity. If transformation activity was not
progressed, the Council would struggle to meet its commitments to
regulatory bodies risking statutory breaches, local and national
reputational damage and potential intervention. The quality of
services would not improve and children, young people, and families
risk experiencing increased delays and reduced access to effective,
value for money, services. Financial modelling indicated that
continuing without transformation would heighten financial risk.
The growing demand for SEND services presented a strong likelihood
that the SEND budget would be significantly overspent, reinforcing
the need for targeted transformation. This option was therefore
dismissed.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)          
that delegate authority is given to the Executive
Director, Children and Education in consultation with the Executive
Director – Finance and Transformation and S151 Officer to
undertake a procurement exercise through the ESPO Framework 664_25
using a mini-competition and to award a contract for the
appointment of a service provider to support transformation
activity to improve the provision of SEND services;
 
(2)          
that the Service Director – Governance is
authorised to execute any documents necessary to give effect to the
proposal in recommendation 2.1 above in consultation with the
Executive Director – Finance and Transformation and the
Executive Director for Children and Education.
topline: The UK council has decided to approve recommendations for the SEND Transformation and improvement of services to address the rising demand for specialist support.

purpose:
Winter Operational Plan to carry out
precautionary treatment of the highway during winter.
content:
Approval was sought for the Highways Winter Operation Plan
2025-2026. Sandwell highways were the arteries of communities. They
connected residents to employment, education, local services and
the wider world. They enabled economic growth, social mobility and
were vital in ensuring good health outcomes. Highways plaid an
important role in the life of a community, particularly the
positive opportunities that they can bring from social inclusion
and interaction.
 
Getting the Highway Winter Operational Plan wrong would
reduced
economic and physical activity resulting from residents being less
likely to travel as well as higher costs for users of the highway
from increased wear and tear and accident damage.
 

Reason for Decision
Road
users and the wider community placed a high value on keeping
traffic moving safely in snow and freezing winter weather. Failure
to do so can result in adverse economic and social impacts, public
dissatisfaction and significant reputational damage.
 
The
Council had a statutory duty ‘to ensure, so far as reasonably
practicable, that safe passage along a highway was not endangered
by snow or ice’. The duty was not absolute, but decisions
were required be taken on reasonable grounds with due care and
regard to relevant considerations set out in best practice
guidance. To meet this duty, winter service operations were carried
out to prevent ice forming (precautionary salting), melt ice
already formed (post salting) and remove snow accumulations by
using ground rock salt which is stored at Taylors Lane Depot in
Oldbury.
 

Alternative Options Considered
There
was no recommended affordable alternative to mitigate the safety
risks addressed by the Winter Operational Plan 2025-26.
 
Resolved that approval is given to the
Highways Winter Maintenance Operational Plan 2025-26.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Highways Winter Maintenance Operational Plan 2025-26.

purpose:
This report seeks endorsement of the Bus
Service Improvement Plan (BSIP) Future Routes programme being
promoted by Transport for West Midlands (TfWM) and ‘in
principle’ approval to take forward corridor BC18 and
corridor BC27.
content:
Approval was sought for the Bus Service Improvement
Plan  for the endorsement of future
routes and ‘in principle’ approval to Corridors BC18
and BC27.
 
The
West Midlands Bus Service Improvement Plan was prepared in response
to the Government’s 2021 national bus strategy –
‘Bus Back Better’. It complements the existing West
Midlands Strategic Vision for Bus. This set out four key objectives
for bus service improvement in the metropolitan area:
 
·      
a more sustainable and attractive service
offer;
·      
a consistent, good delivery of the service
offer;
·      
ensuring a good passenger experience for all;
and
·      
reducing environmental impacts.

 
The
Bus Service Improvement Plan envisaged improvements to deliver
significant bus priority infrastructure across all corridors,
including extensive bus lanes where road space permits.
 
Cabinet Members welcomed the proposals, the increased public
transport offer would continue to benefit residents in Sandwell
enabling the reduction in congestion on the roads and improving
traffic flow through the borough.
 

Reason for Decision
Consultants working on behalf of Transport for West Midlands
were developing proposals on the Core Bus Network to form a
pipeline of shovel-ready schemes to achieve Bus Service Improvement
Plan ambitions. A total of 29 corridors in the Black Country had
been initially reviewed and following a two-stage sifting exercise,
five routes had been shortlisted for taking forward to the
Programme Business Case. Two of these routes, Black Country (BC)18
and BC27, ran through Sandwell.
 
The
BC18 Preferred Strategy includes potential interventions in the
following locations;
·      
Halesowen Street Bus Stops, Oldbury;
·      
A4099 / Beeches Road / Cocksheds Lane Junction;
·      
A4034 / Station Road / Britannia Road
Junction;
·      
A4034 / Mincing Lane / Penncricket Lane Junction;
·      
Church Street / Birmingham Street / Halesowen Street
Junction;
·      
A4034 / Fountain Lane / Broadwell Road
Junction;
·      
exit from West Bromwich Bus Station and Moor Street
/ West Bromwich Ringway;
·      
Wilford Road / All Saints Way Junction;
and
·      
Bromford Lane / Brandon Way Roundabout.
 
Interventions being considered can include the
following;
·      
revised bus stop arrangements;
·      
upgrades to signal phasing and technology to improve
overall traffic flow;
·      
revised junction layouts including potential
replacement of roundabouts with traffic signals to prioritise bus
movements; and
·      
alterations to Traffic Regulation Orders and revised
car parking arrangements to prioritise bus movements.
 
The
BC27 Preferred Strategy included potential interventions in the
following locations;
·      
West Bromwich Bus Station;
·      
West Bromwich High Street;
·      
Carters Green;
·      
Claypit Lane to Bilhay
Lane;
·      
Great Bridge Street;
·      
B4157;
·      
Dudley Street; and
·      
Great Bridge Roundabout.
 
Interventions being considered can include the
following;
·      
changes to internal bus station layout;
·      
relocation of bus stops;
·      
introduction of bus lanes;
·      
upgrades to pedestrian crossings;
·      
signalising junctions to prioritise bus
movements;
·      
additional waiting restrictions; and
·      
alterations to parking arrangements.
 

Alternative Options Considered
The
BC18 and BC27 corridors were chosen by Transport for West Midlands
based on a data driven evaluation, scoring corridors on
socio-demographics, patronage and frequency, safety and
accessibility, delay and congestion, stakeholder support, and
future development. Following the Programme Business Case
submission and approval, further design and consultation would be
conducted.
 
At
each of the intervention locations, alternative layouts had been,
or would be considered, through the design process with the option
providing the most benefits to bus users whilst not disadvantaging
other road users, particularly pedestrians and cyclists.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1) 
that approval is given to the Bus Service
Improvement Plan programme of future corridor improvements as shown
on the Black Country Core Network at Appendix 1;

 
(2) 
that approval is given ‘in principle’ to
the proposed highways interventions within Sandwell that form part
of the Bus Service Improvement Plan Future Routes Programme
Business Case BC18 – Walsall – West Bromwich –
Hayley Green as shown at Appendix 3;
 
(3) 
that approval is given ‘in principle’ to
the proposed highways interventions that form part of the Bus
Service Improvement Plan Future Routes Programme Business Case BC27
– Great Bridge - West Bromwich as shown at Appendix
4;
 
(4) 
that delegated authority is given to the Cabinet

topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Bus Service Improvement Plan for future routes and highways interventions in Sandwell

purpose:
To update cabinet around current status with
the Commercialisation process.
content:
The
Council was due to procure a partner/ investor for development of a
heat network in and around the centre of West Bromwich (potential
extension to Smethwick), with a target launch of the procurement
process prior to April 2026.
 
Once
selected, the partner and the Council would form a delivery
vehicle, typically known as an Energy Services Company (ESCO) to
manage further technical and commercial development, resolve all
relevant financial and contractual measures and launch the detailed
design, construction, and operational phases of the
scheme.
 

Reason for Decision
Switching to a Golden Share Joint Venture (JV) model from the
original envisaged 50:50 Joint Venture would reduce the
Council’s influence over the development of planned heat
network scheme. This was because the Council would not become a
full shareholder under the delivery vehicle, would not be an
investor with associated share capital, and by extension would not
gain from any future investment returns. However, a ‘Golden
Share’ model represented an appropriate alternative as this
mitigates exposure to financial risk for the Council.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – Council-owned Energy Services Company (ESCO), the ESCO
being a “Special Purpose Vehicle” (SPV). This option
would deliver full control to the Council of the delivery of a heat
network but would introduce substantial commercial and financial
risk and require significant financial and resourcing contributions
over an extended period of years. This option introduced an
unacceptable level of financial exposure and risk and was therefore
dismissed.
 
Option
2 – Joint Venture ESCO (where the SPV was owned by two or
more entities, typically combining public and private). This option
would still deliver significant control to the Council of the
delivery of a heat network but would again introduce substantial
commercial and financial risk and require significant financial and
resourcing contributions over an extended period of years. This
option introduced an unacceptable level of financial exposure and
risk and was therefore dismissed.
 
Option
3 – Concession arrangement. This option offered only limited
direct risks albeit a delivery strategy would have to be agreed by
the Council. The Council would also have a commissioning role and
would be ‘provider of last resort’. Further additional
risks included no, or limited control over project beyond
concession commission, potential of non-delivery and that only
selective (the most profitable elements only) would be delivered.
This option offered an inappropriate financial, commercial and
legal risk profile for the council and was therefore
dismissed.
 
Option
4 – Do nothing. This option offered a range of benefits which
included no risk to the Council. This would however limit the
ability of the Council to influence any proposals other than
through the formal planning and regulatory processes. This option
was therefore dismissed.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1) 
that delegated authority is given to the Executive
Director Place in consultation with the Executive Director of
Finance and Transformation and the Cabinet Member for Regeneration
and Infrastructure, to:-

 
a)   
proceed with the Commercialisation stage and procure
a Development Partner with a delivery model based on a
‘Golden Share’ arrangement;

 
b)   
submit a revised Green Heat Network Fund application
requesting further funding to support a Commercialisation process
covering a heat supply option to Smethwick and the City of
Birmingham and including a request for further capital funding;
 
c)   
consider the outcome of a borough-wide Heat Network
Zoning study (when completed), in conjunction with anticipated
National Heat Network Zoning Regulations and ensure any appropriate
measures are put in place to support a West Bromwich/Smethwick Heat
Network and de-risk the project where possible.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to proceed with a 'Golden Share' Joint Venture model for the development of a heat network in West Bromwich and potentially Smethwick.

purpose:
To present the Plan for Neighbourhoods
Programme Regeneration Plan prior to submitting to MHCLG in
November 2025.
content:
Approval was sought for the proposed outline of the Smethwick
10-year Regeneration Plan as developed by the Smethwick Partnership
Board, prior to it being to be submitted to the Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local Government.
 
The
Smethwick Partnership Board functioned as the Neighbourhood Board
for the programme, in addition to overseeing the Smethwick Town
Deal Programme (£23.5m Towns Fund Programme). The Smethwick
Partnership Board had worked in partnership with Sandwell Council
to develop the plans.
 
Cabinet Members emphasised the importance of community in
decision making and how working in partnership allowed for greater
engagement. Working in partnership was something Sandwell was good
at and which had been demonstrated in previous schemes.
 

Reason for Decision
On 4
March 2025, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local
Government announced the Plan for Neighbourhoods Programme, through
which Smethwick was set to benefit from up to £20 million
investment over 10-years. The programme aimed to deliver long-term,
community-led regeneration through local Neighbourhood Boards
working alongside local authorities.
 
Each
Board was required to produce a 10-year Regeneration Plan, setting
out the vision and priorities, and a 4-year investment plan,
providing further detail on early-stage delivery. Both plans would
be submitted by 28 November 2025.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option
1 – not to submit the plan. Submission of the Regeneration
Plan was a mandatory requirement for Smethwick to access the
£20 million funding allocation. The Ministry of Housing,
Communities and Local Government had advised the Neighbourhood
Boards that they were encouraged to work closely with the
Accountable Body to develop plans that accurately reflected
community needs. This option was dismissed to ensure access to the
funding is maintained to deliver regeneration for the local
area.
 
Option
2 – maintain existing decision-making arrangements. For
project applications that exceed £1m, the current approach
would have been to maintain the Council’s existing process,
which required Cabinet approval. However, this approach could
affect delivery timelines, as the lead in period for Cabinet papers
may not align with the milestones and deadlines set by the
Smethwick Partnership Board and Programme. Retaining this process
could therefore delay project approvals, potentially slow delivery
and reduce the programme’s overall effectiveness. This option
was dismissed.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1) 
that approval is given to the draft Regeneration
Plan and delegate authority is given to the Service Director
Governance Monitoring Officer, in consultation with the Service
Director Economy and Regeneration, the Executive Director of
Finance and Transformation and the Cabinet Member for Regeneration
and Infrastructure to make any minor technical amendments and
submit the Plan to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local
Government (MHCLG);

 
(2) 
that delegated authority is given to the Service
Director Governance Monitoring Officer, in consultation with the
Service Director Economy and Regeneration, the Executive Director
of Finance and Transformation and the Cabinet Member for
Regeneration and Infrastructure, authorised to –
 
a)   
sign off technical amendments to the Regeneration
Plan during the confirmation stage (the period following submission
of the Plan and receiving a Memorandum of Understanding from
MHCLG);

 
b)   
review and formally accept the Plan for
Neighbourhoods Memorandum of Understanding from Ministry of
Housing, Communities and Local Government.
 
(3) 
that approval is given for the establishment of an
Assurance Panel comprising the Cabinet Portfolio Holder for
Regeneration and Infrastructure, the S151 Officer, an SIU
representative, and nominees from the Smethwick Partnership Board
and delegate authority to the Assurance Panel to approve projects
over £1 million, in accordance with Sandwell Council’s
responsibility as Accountable Body and following the governance
model of the Sandwell Towns Fund Programme.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Smethwick 10-year Regeneration Plan for submission to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government

purpose:
To receive an update on progress of the
delivery of the Levelling Up Partnership and to approve updated to
the Wednesbury Levelling Up Partnership Board Terms of
Reference
content:
Consideration was
given to the progress of delivering against the objectives of the
Levelling Up Partnership Programme over the past six months which
included:-
·     
Phase 1 Green Spaces projects main work completion (Balls Hill,
Lakeside and Norbury and Wyntor Lane Open Spaces)??and publicity
launch;
·     
community safety capital works (new and upgraded CCTV, business
radio link, nuisance bike measures) and publicity launch;
·     
main phase of Public Realm works in Wednesbury Town Centre and
publicity launch;
·     
Development Partner appointment for Friar Park Urban Village
project.
 
Other achievements
and milestones included:-
·     
Planning approval granted for Hydes Road Pavilion demolition and
rebuild;
·     
final stages of preparation for building improvement scheme,
art/mural project, wayfinding, and further public realm works in
Wednesbury Town Centre;
·     
final stages of preparation for start on site at Friar Park
Millennium Centre.
 
Over the period up to
end August 2025, there were two projects with a significant level
of risk, slippage and/or issues; Friar Park Urban Village Land
Remediation Project and Green spaces: Hydes Road. 
 
Following an annual
review of Wednesbury Levelling Up Partnership Board membership in
August 2025 to ensure continuous improvement in the programme
governance arrangement
 
approval was now
sought to the revised terms of reference of the Board which would
ensure consistency with the Town Deal Boards’ Terms of
Reference and include provision for the Chair’s appointment
process.
 
Cabinet Members
welcomed the update and the progress it demonstrated, emphasising
the successful visits that had been undertaken by members to
Wednesbury town centre and tram station where they had been able to
engage with residents and local businesses, the redevelopment of
Balls Hill open space had also been welcomed after enhancing the
local area improving access and amenities. The Wednesbury Levelling
Up Partnership Board was thanked for its commitment to the competed
and ongoing programmes and emphasised how it had brought together
the local community.
 

Reason for Decision
In September 2023,
details of the Levelling Up Partnership (£20.4m) were
formally announced by Government. Approval was sought to establish
governance arrangements, approve the target geography as
Wednesbury, and to agree the set of projects as follows:-
·     
Friar Park Urban Village 
·     
Wednesbury Community Safety Scheme  
·     
Wednesbury Town Centre Improvements  
·     
Wednesbury Greenspaces Improvements  
·     
Friar Park Millennium Centre expansion 
 

Alternative Options Considered
The proposed updates
to the Wednesbury Levelling Up Partnership (WLUP) Board Terms of
Reference had been compiled as part of continuous improvement and
ensuring consistency across the WLUP Board and other Regeneration
Boards.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that details of the progress to date on delivering the aims and
objectives of the Levelling Up Partnership be received and
endorsed;

 
(2)         
that approval is given to the revised Wednesbury Levelling Up
Partnership Board Terms of reference as set out in Appendix A.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations for the progress of the Levelling Up Partnership Programme.

content:
The Cabinet received
details of the Quarter 1 Corporate Performance Report 2025/26 and
approval was sought for the targets for Corporate Performance
Indicators.
 
The Council’s
Performance Management Framework enabled the Council to track
progress in delivering the strategic outcomes in the Council Plan,
improve services through identifying poor performance and sharing
good practice, celebrate our achievements and provide a strong
evidence base for improved decision making and the efficient use of
resources. Through enabling the Council to identify opportunities
for continuous improvement, the Performance Management Framework
was also a key component in the Council’s journey to becoming
an outstanding organisation.
 

Reason for Decision
Performance measures
for 2025/26 were reviewed and amended where appropriate and were
aligned against the outcomes under each strategic theme, which,
along with the updates to the business plan actions, would allow
the Council to understand how it was delivering against the Council
Plan. Progress was reported on a quarterly and annual basis through
the Corporate Performance Report.
 
Performance of key
contracts was included in the quarterly performance reports to
provide oversight of the performance of these services and
assurance that contract management mechanisms continue to be in
place and effective.
 
The information
collected was used to enable the authority to better understand the
impact of its work on local people, and where necessary, target
actions and resources to improve progress in achieving the
Council’s strategic objectives.
 
Cabinet Members
emphasised the work of the Children’s Services and Education
directorate, highlighting how Sandwell had been chosen as a piolet
area for a Department for Education Learn and Grow programme, which
would support young people with SEND when they reach 16 and were
finishing school accessing education, employment or training. In
addition, Sandwell had also been selected to pilot the Department
for Education Local Authority Partner for Severe Absence, that
would help the Council understand options for addressing absence
across schools.
 
Work continued to
enhance the local offer for those children and young people with
SEND. Additional resources had been provided to the Connor Centre
in West Bromwich to enable the centre to be utilised more
effectively in service delivery. The enhanced centre would work to
provide in borough support and education with the aim of reducing
out of borough placements.
 
In recognition of the
work that Children’s Services provided, the Youth Service
team had been shortlisted for the Workforce Development Award at
the Children’s and Young People Now Awards 2025. The
nomination recognised the work of the youth service team to
support, protect and empower children and young people in
Sandwell.
 

Alternative Options Considered
There were no
alternative options to consider.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that details of the progress on the further development of the
Corporate Performance Management Framework be received;
 
(2)         
That approval is given to the 2025/26 Quarter 1 monitoring
reports;
 
(3)         
that approval is given to the targets for Corporate Performance
Indicators;
 
(4)         
that approval is given for the removal of two Performance
Indicators from the Corporate Set and the replacement of one
Performance Indicator with another, as set out in appendix B.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve targets for Corporate Performance Indicators for the Council's Performance Management Framework.

purpose:
This report seeks to obtain delegated
authority for the renewal of the Oracle Fusion Support
contract.
content:
Approval was sought
for the Oracle Fusion Managed Service Provider for a 3-year period
with the option to extend for 1-year.
 
The Council received
Oracle Fusion support services from Infosys, its existing Managed
Service Provider. Infosys had supported the Council through the
initial Oracle Fusion implementation programme, providing
early-life support and helping to stabilise the Oracle Fusion
system.
 
The current Managed
Service Provider contract enabled the provision of support and
enhancements for the following Oracle Fusion modules: ERP, EPM,
Procurement, HCM, Integrations, Reporting and Risk Management
Cloud. Infosys initially provided tier 1 (low level), tier 2
(mid-level) and tier 3 (technical) support, however, tier 1 and tier 2 support were now
provided in-house within the Council. Infosys continued to provide
tier 3 support and aimed to resolve 60-80 support
‘tickets’ (predominantly incidents) per month.
 
The current Managed
Service Provider contract ended on 31 December 2025. To ensure
optimum quality and effectiveness of Managed Service Provider
support going forward, a process to re-tender the contract was
being carried out, to allow all appropriate suppliers the chance to
bid for the work. It was proposed that a new support contract would
formally begin on 1 January 2026 for an initial term of three
years, with the option to extend for a further one year. If, under
the new contract, the appointed Managed Service Provider was any
organisation other than the existing Managed Service Provider, it
was proposed that the new contract would include a transition
period from 3 November 2025 to 31 December 2025, to ensure a smooth
handover of services from the existing provider to the new
provider.
 

Reason for Decision
The Oracle Fusion
platform was critical to the Council’s financial and
operational systems. Continued support through a Managed Service
Provider was essential to maintain service continuity, ensure
system stability and support future upgrades or changes.
 
The contract to be
let was for managed support relating to all
of the Oracle Fusion modules that had been implemented at
the Council. The new contractor would be required to provide tier 3
support for incidents, change requests and reporting. They would
also be required to manage the mandatory quarterly patching on
behalf of the Council and to provide strategic advice on the use
of, and enhancements of, Oracle Fusion across the Council. The
Council anticipated that the volume of ‘tickets’ to be
resolved would be approximately 110 per month, made up of
approximately 100 incidents, 5-10 change requests and up to 5
reports. The Council had ambitions to work in collaboration with
the winning bidder to work in a shift-left mentality which would
enable increasing the first-time fix rate at tier 1 and 2 levels,
therefore reducing the volume of tickets which would go across to
the Managed Service Provider.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Several alternative
options were considered as part of the planning for this
procurement:
 
Option 1 - Extend the
existing contract with the current Managed Support Provider.
The current Managed
Support Provider also supported the Council through the initial
implementation of Oracle Fusion and through the hypercare period. To evidence ongoing value for
money it was important to enter a competitive process for further
support requirements at the expiry of the current contract. This
also provided the opportunity to review service levels, enable
innovation and ensure alignment with the Council’s strategic
goals.
 
Option 2 - Bring the
service fully in-house.
Managing Oracle
Fusion support entirely in-house was considered but ruled out. The
Council did not have the specialist technical capability or
capacity to manage the full service internally. Doing so would also
carry significant risks to service continuity, performance and
compliance.
 
Option 3 - Procure
via open market tender.
An open market
procurement process was considered but not pursued. The decision to
use the Government’s G-Cloud 14 framework ensured a
compliant, faster, and more efficient route to market. It also
provided access to a wide range of pre-approved suppliers with
relevant experience in the public sector and in managed service
provision.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that delegated authority is given to the Executive Director for
Finance and Transformation (Section 151 Officer) to undertake a G
Cloud 14 Framework call-off process to appoint a Managed Service
Provider for Oracle Fusion Support for a 3-year period with the
option to extend for 1-year;

 
(2)         
that delegated authority is given for the Executive Director for
Finance and Transformation (Section 151 Officer) in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources to award and
enter into a new contract and any associated documentation for the
provision of a Managed Service Provider for Oracle Fusion for a
period of 3 years with the option to extend services for 1 further
period of up to 1 year, on terms to be agreed by the Executive
Director for Finance and Transformation (S151 Officer);

 
(3)         
that approval is given to the Service Director for Governance
(Monitoring Officer) to execute any documents necessary to give
effect to the proposals referred to in Resolution (1) and (2)
above.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to appoint a new Managed Service Provider for Oracle Fusion support for a 3-year period with the option to extend for 1 year.

purpose:
To consider the Medium Term Financial
Strategy.
content:
Details of the Autumn
2025 Medium Term Financial Strategy was considered and approval was sought to commence
consultation on a range of proposed efficiency and income
generation options sufficient to offset forecast increases in
expenditure in 2026/would support the Council in setting a balanced
budget in February 2026.
 
The Council
commissioned children’s social care services from its
wholly-owned company, Sandwell
Children’s Trust. Historically the Council and the Trust had
agreed a one-year contract sum to be paid for services in advance
of the beginning of each financial year.
 
In recent years, the
Trust had been operating at a deficit, as a
result of increased costs of residential care placements and
increased demand for services, particularly for complex services.
This was a position being reported by councils across the country.
At the end of 2024/25, the deficit built up by the Trust had grown
to £19.792m.
 
Within the
Council’s MTFS, it was proposed to provide the Trust with a
three-year contract sum for the financial years 2025/26 to 2027/28,
to improve financial planning for both the Council and the
Trust; providing certainty of
expenditure for the Council and certainty of income for the Trust.
The proposed three-year contract sum intended not only to provide a
viable and sustainable level of income for the Trust over the three
years, but it would also provide sufficient funding to offset the
cumulative deficit built up to the end of the 2024/25 financial
year.
 
Approval was also
sought to recommend Council to approve a three-year contract sum to
be paid to Sandwell Children’s Trust for the period 1 April
2025 to 31 March 2028.
 

Reason for Decision
The Medium-Term
Financial Strategy (MTFS) showed how the Council could deploy
resources to achieve its strategic objectives, as set out in the
Council Plan. It showed how expenditure and income budgets must
change to ensure services were adequate to address local need and
meet financial pressures from inflation and increasing demand.
 
The immediate
objective of the updated MTFS was focused on achieving a balanced
budget for 2026/27 whilst protecting services provided to
vulnerable children and adults.
 

Alternative Options Considered
The Council was
legally required to set a balanced budget by March each year. There
were no legal alternative options other than to consult on a range
of expenditure reductions and/or income generation measures that
achieve a balanced budget for the General Fund.
 
In relation to the
proposed contract sum to be paid to Sandwell Children’s
Trust, the Trust had no reserves and was unable to take sufficient
action to offset its financial deficit built up to the end of the
2024/25 financial year.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)                 
that the Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy be endorsed, as set
out at Appendix 1, that includes financial estimates and proposals
that could achieve the legal requirement to balance the
Council’s budget for 2026/27;
 
(2)                 
that Cabinet receive the figures in the Draft Medium-Term Financial
Strategy that are accurate as at October
2025;
 
(3)                 
that approval is given to the Executive Director for Finance and
Transformation to commence a period of appropriate consultation on
the Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy proposals detailed at
Annex 3 of Appendix C;
 
(4)                 
that Cabinet endorse the budget timetable as set out in Annex 1 of
Draft Medium-Term Financial Strategy;
 


(5)                 
that the Council be recommended to approve the three-year contract
sum, with a total value of £309.072m, to be paid to Sandwell
Children’s Trust for the contract period 1 April 2025 to 31
March 2028.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a three-year contract sum of £309.072m to be paid to Sandwell Children's Trust to offset their financial deficit and ensure financial planning for both the Council and the Trust.

purpose:
To seek approval to implement the
recommendations of moving the procurement of equipment in house
within JES.
content:
Approval was sought
to transfer the procurement of equipment back to an in-house
solution within the Joint Equipment Store. Since joining the
Croydon Integrated Hub framework in 2013, the Council had not fully
evaluated the continued value for money. The Joint Equipment Store
Team had reviewed the current position and looked at a number of options that were available to them with
the development of new frameworks but also with changes in the
marketplace. In line with the Council’s value for money
review, the Team had completed a detailed analysis of the current
model against other available frameworks. This comparison detailed
that there were savings to be achieved through bringing the service
in-house. As a minimum, the Joint Equipment Team would be able to
achieve a 9.5% saving on the standard equipment purchased.
 
Cabinet Members
confirmed that the Croydon Integrated Hub would continue to be used
in order to provide bespoke equipment to
ensure those with complex needs continue to receive the support
they require.
 

Reason for Decision
The current
procurement framework had been in place since 2013. The equipment
that was being procured had seen a gradual year on year increase in
the equipment that was procured. The contract value was £1
million when it started and had risen to £1.9 million in
2024/25. Whilst regular meetings had been held, there had not been
a deep dive into the procurement model and exercise to validate it
was still providing value for money for the Council. The management
fee that had been paid had not been reviewed since 2013.
 
In addition to the
increased spend, there had also been a shift in the percentage of
standard and non-standard equipment. There was now a position where
there was an approximate 50% balance between standard and
non-standard equipment which meant Adult Social Care were not
benefiting from any special prices and paying the market rate plus
a 9.5% management fee on the equipment that was purchased.
 
The proposal was to
bring this service in-house and manage the whole end to end process
in the Joint Equipment Store.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Option 1: Bring
Procurement In-House (Recommended). Under this option, the Council
would terminate routine use of the Croydon Framework and bring the
full procurement function in-house within the JES. The Council
would directly manage procurement activities, including sourcing,
ordering, and supplier liaison. To support this transition, two
additional Business Support Officers would be recruited. Existing
management structures would remain in place. This model allowed for
greater local control, improved responsiveness, and potential cost
savings through direct supplier engagement.
 
Option 2: Negotiate
Reduced Management Fee with Croydon. This option involved seeking a
reduction in the 9.5% management fee while continuing to use the
Croydon Framework. However, Croydon had confirmed that there was no
intention to revise the fee. The benefits of staying in the
Framework were therefore outweighed by the lack of pricing
flexibility, particularly given that approximately 50% of equipment
now falls outside the standard catalogue.
 
Option 3: Transition
to NHS-C Framework. This model explored transitioning procurement
to the NHS-C Framework. While this route benefited from being
publicly procured and compliant, detailed analysis identified that
the NHS-C Framework lacked a comprehensive equipment catalogue and
would not support the JES operational requirements. Furthermore,
cost comparisons of the top 50 high-volume standard items showed no
material savings.
 
Option 4: Use YPO
Framework for Standard Items Only. This option involved using the
YPO (Yorkshire Purchasing Organisation) Framework to procure only
standard items, while the JES team would independently source all
non-standard and specialist items. Although this hybrid model could
offer partial savings, it added complexity and potential
inefficiencies through dual procurement routes.
 
Option 5: Do Nothing.
Retaining the current model without change would avoid disruption
but would perpetuate poor value for money. Given that half of all
equipment was now non-standard and subject to full retail pricing,
with an added 9.5% management fee, this option was not sustainable.
It also maintained operational constraints that would hinder
service flexibility.
 

Resolved:-
 
(1)         
that delegated authority is given to the Executive Director for
Adult Social Care and Health to move forward with bringing the
Joint Equipment Service end-to-end service delivery in-house;

 
(2)         
that delegated authority is given to the Executive Director for
Adult Social Care and Health to approve the recruitment of 2 x
Business Support Officers to manage the additional requirements and
demand on the Team as a result of
bringing in the Joint Equipment Service end-to-end service
delivery 
in-house.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to bring the procurement of equipment back in-house to achieve cost savings and improve efficiency.

purpose:
To consider the Housing and Asset Management
Policies:
• Damp and Mould Policy
• Tree Policy
content:
Approval was sought
for the Housing and Asset Management Policies. The Damp and Mould
Policy had been developed in line with the requirements of
Awaab’s Law, which ensured that damp and mould hazards were
identified, reported, and resolved within strict timescales to
protect residents’ health. In addition, the tree works for
Council Housing Properties Policy set out a clear framework for the
safe and responsible management of trees on Council housing land,
balancing resident safety with environmental sustainability.
 

Reason for Decision
Damp and Mould
Policy
Sandwell Council was
committed to ensuring that all residents lived in warm, dry, and
safe homes, free from damp, mould, and condensation. The Damp and
Mould Policy set out how the Council would prevent, investigate,
and resolve problems quickly, protecting residents’ health
and wellbeing. This policy would allow the Council to:-
 
·     
act swiftly on reports of damp and mould, with clear timescales for
inspections and repairs;
·     
maintain homes in line with Awaab’s Law, the Housing Health
and Safety Rating System, and the Decent Homes Standard;
·     
support residents by taking responsibility for resolving issues
without placing blame;
·     
reduce long-term risks through proactive maintenance and
investment;
·     
build trust by being transparent, keeping residents informed, and
prioritising safety.
 
Tree Works for
Council Housing Properties Policy.
Sandwell Council
recognised the importance of trees in creating safe, attractive,
and sustainable housing environments. The Tree Works Policy
outlined how the Council would manage and maintain trees on Council
housing land, balancing safety, environmental benefits, and
residents’ needs. This policy would allow the Council
to:-
 
·     
protect tenants and their homes by prioritising works on dangerous,
dead, dying, or diseased trees;
·     
safeguard and enhance the environment by caring for healthy trees
and encouraging biodiversity;
·     
provide clear guidance on tenant and Council responsibilities for
tree maintenance;
·     
ensure fair, consistent decisions on when and how tree works will
be carried out;
·     
promote sustainable neighbourhoods by managing trees responsibly in
both private gardens and communal areas.
 

Alternative Options Considered
Not seek adoption for
the two policies.  This would result in
not delivering the objectives of the Housing Strategy 2023 –
2028, Asset Management Strategy 2024-2029, Housing Repairs and
Maintenance Policy and the Regulatory Housing Standards that came
into effect in April 2024. Therefore, this would result in the
sub-optimal management of our Housing Services. This option was
therefore dismissed.
 
Resolved:-

 
(1)         
that approval is given to the adoption of the following housing
management policy documents:

purpose:
Additional special school places are required
in Sandwell for children with an Education, Health and Care Plan.
The Meadows School agreed to provide a satellite centre for Post 16
at Connor Education Centre. As part of the reconfiguration the West
Bromwich North Family Hub, the existing male toilets and kitchen
facilities have been incorporated into the school’s
accommodation, on the basis that the West Bromwich North Family Hub
would remain closed.

West Bromwich North Family Hub will however re-open to the public,
and to enable re-opening the remaining toilet needs to be
reconfigured to provide male, female and assisted toilets. The
remaining kitchen needs to be refitted to provide suitable amenity
space for staff.

At The Meadows School new Post 16 Hub, during the recent
refurbishment works a series of contract variations have resulted
in additional costs being incurred.

The Department for Education (DfE) has allocated additional capital
funding to Local Authority’s to support the introduction of
new special school places, High Needs Provision Capital Allocation
(HNPCA). The proposed works will be funded from the Council’s
HNPCA allocation as they are required to complete reconfiguration
of the accommodation to provide additional school places.

Connor Education Centre (a former Primary School) has been held in
the Children and Education portfolio for a significant number of
years. Since closing as a school, the building had been occupied by
a private nursery, WBNFH and office space for the SEN and Inclusive
Learning Teams, Inclusive Learning Services.

Part of the building was reconfigured in 2022 as a temporary
solution for Elm Tree Primary Academy to ensure the new school
could open on time as the DfE were unable to deliver the new build
until September 2023. In September 2023, following vacation by the
Academy, this area was made available to Albright Education Centre
to provide additional Alternative Provision places.

Individual Cabinet member decision “The Meadows School -
satellite centre for Post 16 Connor Centre refurbishment”
dated 16 June 2025 authorised the reconfiguration of the remaining
Inclusive Learning Services spaces for The Meadows School to
provide additional Special School places at Post 16.

Barnardo's, the council’s appointed provider for West
Bromwich North Family Hub, no longer require office space at the
site, but will continue to provide community outreach and support
services from Connor Road. The office space will be used as
drop-down space for council staff, and Barnardo’s staff when
on site delivering community outreach and support.

To achieve the most appropriate accommodation for The Meadows
School, part of the West Bromwich North Family Hub accommodation
has been included in the school’s accommodation.

The West Bromwich North Family Hub has been temporarily closed and
services provided from other family hubs in the area during the
building works for The Meadows School.

West Bromwich North Family Hub has one remaining toilet. For
Barnardo’s to reopen and provide community services the
remaining toilet needs to be reconfigured to provide male, female
and assisted toilets.

The remaining kitchen needs to be refitted to provide suitable
amenity space for West Bromwich North Family Hub and council
staff.

Speller Metcalf is the appointed contractor for the works at Connor
Education Centre. The contract will be extended to include the
works at West Bromwich North Family Hub. The contract was awarded
following a procurement exercise conducted through the Constructing
West Midlands (CWM) framework. It is recommended that extension to
the existing contract to include these minor works is more cost
effective and timely to the council than undertaking a separate
procurement exercise to complete the project.

During the reconfiguration of The Connor Centre for the purposes of
The Meadows School, six variations to the contract were
required.
